articles.title: 'This is a disaster': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat
articles.summary: Some Republicans tell the BBC the president's focus on his legacy and indifference to voter concerns cost them.
articles.body:
Inside the Republican Party, initial shock at the stunning election results on Tuesday night quickly gave way to anger with US President Donald Trump.

After Democrats won upset after upset in deep-red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina, some Republicans focused their ire on Trump, arguing that his focus on his legacy and indifference to voter concerns cost the party control of Congress.

"It's on him. It's not on anybody else. It's a total, complete rejection of President Trump," Bill Miller, a top Republican lobbyist in Texas, told the BBC. "This is a disaster of the first magnitude. Nobody saw it coming like this."

Most Republicans expected to lose control of the House and were clear-eyed about the challenge of holding onto the Senate in a tough election cycle that favoured the party out of power.

But some said in interviews that Trump dragged them down with unpopular policies, a low job approval rating and obsession over construction projects in Washington.

"It was just one mistake after another," said Gregg Peppin, a Republican strategist in Minnesota. "Clearly, in state after state, people did not like the president's policies."

A White House ally said public disapproval with Trump over the Iran war, tariffs and the administration's immigration crackdown created a "perfect storm" in November.

"There's palpable frustration [within] the party about how this has all played out," the person said, and much of it is directed at Trump. Anger with Trump "is extremely high".

The BBC spoke to a dozen party operatives, campaign officials, White House allies and others, many of whom spoke on background to offer a candid assessment of Trump's approach to the midterms.

Trump and Republicans had a lot riding on the outcome on Tuesday night. A stronger showing by the president's party - as happened in 2022, when Democrats under then-President Joe Biden lost just nine seats in the House, and gained one in the Senate - would have given Republicans some momentum heading into 2028.

But Trump will instead face a motivated Democratic majority in Congress that is eager to investigate the administration, block his judicial nominees and stymie the rest of his agenda.

The midterms have ushered in an uncertain new phase in Trump's second term and may force Republicans to start grappling with their post-Trump future.

"I don't think his influence is slipping," said Steve Scheffler, the Republican National Committeeman in Iowa, speaking on the eve of the election. Still, he said, when it came to the midterms, "there were things you wish he said differently".

Trump was silent for much of the night before posting a message on Truth Social after the House and Senate were called for Democrats.

"I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter," Trump wrote.

He said in later interviews with the New York Times and Fox News that he would accept the election results. Trump told Fox he was a "little bit surprised" by the election results, but noted that the president's party typically fared poorly in midterm elections.

Since 1934, the party in the White House has only gained seats in three midterm elections. While the Democratic gains in 2026 did not set a record, the party did win dozens of House races, state governor contests and Senate seats, including in states where the party had not been competitive for decades.

Before Tuesday, Democrats had not won a Senate seat in Kansas since 1932, and had not won a statewide race in Texas in more than three decades. The party also notched surprise upsets in other reliably red states like South Carolina that were thought to be safe seats for Republicans just weeks before Election Day.

Trump and Vice-President JD Vance held dozens of campaign rallies in the run-up to the midterms. The principal Trump-aligned Super PAC, MAGA Inc., spent hundreds of millions backing Republican candidates.

Trump allies said it was unfair to hold him responsible for the party's election losses. They pointed to the history of midterm elections, and said the party was saddled with weak Republican candidates in battleground states like Georgia, Michigan and Texas.

Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee in Texas, ran "the worst Senate campaign in the country from either side of the aisle," said another Texas Republican operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. "If Ken's campaign knocked on 100,000 doors I'd be shocked," the source said. The person added that Paxton's victorious Democratic opponent, James Talarico, ran "a really good and smart campaign."

Democrats 'got their wish': Voters react to midterm results

Others defended Trump's autumn campaign schedule, noting that he had to balance his day job of running the country with midterm travel.

"He's the president. He's not going to spend his time campaigning 24/7," said Krish Mathrani, the Michigan Republican Party's youth chair. Mathrani said Trump's campaign rallies helped drive up enthusiasm among Republican voters. "President Trump is a turnout machine," he said.

That's true in presidential elections. But Trump's vaunted turnout operation has failed to deliver in elections when he's not on the ballot, and 2026 proved no different.

Voters rejected Trump's argument that the economy was better on his watch and that he was achieving his aims in the war with Iran. The effort by Trump to portray Democrats as extreme socialists also fell flat, as voters handed victories to moderates like Roy Cooper in North Carolina.

"That just didn't work with Cooper," said a Cooper campaign official. "Trying to tag him as some socialist liberal, that wasn't going to fly."

Trump often seemed disinterested in the midterms over the summer, the period of time when Republicans in Congress shifted their focus to the election.

Trump was consumed by the war with Iran abroad and his construction overhaul of Washington at home. The projects included the under-construction ballroom and a helipad on the South Lawn of the White House, renovations to a local golf course, a proposed memorial arch near Arlington Cemetery and renovations to the Kennedy Center.

Events like a UFC match at the White House on Trump's 80th birthday in June created the impression that the president was more interested in feting himself than winning the midterms, several sources said. Trump also repeatedly downplayed the rising costs of gas and often cast the affordability issue as a Democratic hoax.

Trump turned his full attention to the election in September at the Republican Party's midterm convention. The event was a gamble: Republicans hadn't held a midterm convention in decades, and it was an open question whether voters would tune in.

Trump dominated the convention in Dallas, frustrating Republicans who told the BBC they wanted to highlight the party's midterm candidates.

In his rambling keynote speech, Trump pledged to give $5,000 (£3,700) to Americans if Republicans retained control of Congress and raised eyebrows with an endorsement of Paxton which included a lengthy criticism of the candidate's lack of charisma and physical appearance.

"Obviously, that's never helpful," Robin Armstrong, Texas' Republican National Committeeman, said of Trump's critique of Paxton. "You're not going to stop what President Trump says. We just have to kind of live with that."

The convention failed to attract a large television audience, and Democrats were quick to call it a failure. "It backfired for Republicans because nobody paid any attention to it," said Terri Burke, the Texas Democratic Party's executive director.

Trump's penchant for straying off-message continued when he hit the campaign trail in the final weeks before Election Day. He made headlines for praising Ohio Republican Senator John Husted's physique, and drew criticism for calling Abdul El-Sayed a "jihadist" in the Michigan Senate race.

As Trump criss-crossed the country stumping for Republican candidates, the White House contended with controversies in Washington. Katie Zacharia was ousted after just five days as White House press secretary, and Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned as the US ambassador to Greece after reports surfaced that she asked a donor to pay her credit card debt.

Trump also faced a backlash in October for striking a deal to buy Russian diesel. The agreement, which blindsided members of Congress and drew condemnation from some Republicans, came just weeks after Trump signed a sanctions bill aimed at cutting off Russian oil and gas revenue.

Democrats used the deal and other scandals swirling around the White House to make the case for retaking control of Congress. The messaging resonated in the end, as Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress in convincing fashion.

A second White House ally said that the president's political aides projected optimism until the final days of the election, even as it became clear the party was headed to defeat.

Now, as Republicans take stock of the loss, several said they were ready to look ahead to the 2028 election.

"Whether that's JD Vance, or Marco Rubio, or Ted Cruz, we've got a pretty big bench," said Scheffler, the state's RNC member. "It'll be a wide open race."

Peppin, the Republican strategist, said the midterms results demonstrated the party needed a new direction. "I sincerely hope that we've turned the page from the Trump era, and that we'll have new players, new issues and a new focus moving forward."

articles.title: Democrat drops out of race due to health concerns and still wins; opponent says, 'We deserve to know more'
articles.summary: Democratic Iowa state House candidate Eric Armstrong, who announced in September that he was dropping his campaign due to health struggles, still won the ele...
articles.body:
A Democratic candidate who dropped his campaign for health reasons still defeated the Republican candidate in an Iowa state House race.

Democrat Eric Armstrong explained in a Sept. 7 Facebook post that he was abandoning his campaign due to health issues.

"Running a successful campaign requires immense physical and mental energy. Recently, I have been facing some personal health issues that require my full attention and immediate care," Armstrong wrote, in part.

"Because I must prioritize my health and recovery at this time, I am stepping down from my campaign, effective immediately. This was a deeply difficult choice. However, I know it is the right one.

"Our District deserves a representative who can give 100 percent of their energy to this race. Right now, I must focus on healing so that I can continue to serve our community in other ways in the future."

Despite this announcement, Armstrong's name remained on the ballot, and voters still elected him .

Unofficial results indicate that Armstrong received 4,602 votes, while Republican Keith Jones, who is a member of the Pottawattamie County Board of Supervisors, received 3,737 votes.

"I'm going to do my best to represent" the district, Armstrong said during a phone interview Wednesday with The New York Times . "But I still have health issues. That's what I'm struggling with."

Armstrong did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment Thursday.

In part of a statement to Fox News Digital Thursday, Jones wrote, "I think we deserve to know more."

"Serious rumors were that he was hiding a background that could have disqualified him from office. People 'could have' donated to his campaign and subsequently voted for him based on a falsehood. I was a police officer for 29 years. There's absolutely something there that needs to be investigated by the media," Jones later wrote in part of another statement provided to Fox News Digital on Thursday.

"If he's truly sick, why did he reenter the race? Is he healthy enough to hold office? Did he lie about being sick to cover a damaging personal story? Public trust at that level is important. Is he qualified to be in public office?" Jones asked.

The state House seat is held by Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek, who defeated Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson in the Iowa U.S. Senate race this week.

articles.title: Presidente destituído do Paraguai, Santiago Peña é preso em Assunção | G1
articles.standfirst: O Ministério Público decretou a ordem de prisão assim que o Senado aprovou por unanimidade o impeachment. Peña é suspeito de envolvimento em um escândalo financeiro que levou ao fechamento do maior banco digital do país.
articles.summary: O Ministério Público decretou a ordem de prisão assim que o Senado aprovou por unanimidade o impeachment. Peña é suspeito de envolvimento em um escândalo financeiro que levou ao fechamento do maior banco digital do país.
articles.body:
O presidente destituído do Paraguai , Santiago Peña, foi preso na noite desta sexta-feira (6) em Assunção. O Ministério Público decretou a ordem de prisão assim que o Senado aprovou, por unanimidade, o impeachment dele. Peña é suspeito de envolvimento em um escândalo financeiro que levou ao fechamento do maior banco digital do país. Em Assunção, os enviados especiais César Menezes e Marcelo Benincassa têm as informações.

"Nós estamos aqui na praça que fica exatamente na frente do Congresso, onde o Senado acabou de votar o impeachment do agora ex-presidente do Paraguai Santiago Peña. Imediatamente depois que ele foi destituído, uma grande multidão que está aqui na praça começou a se manifestar. Eles protestam contra o Partido Colorado, que é o partido do ex-presidente e também do vice-presidente, e também pela situação do banco Ueno, porque muitos deles estão com o dinheiro trancado, sem acesso ao dinheiro. Logo depois que o impeachment foi votado, uma sequência de eventos aconteceu. O presidente Peña publicou nas redes sociais que estava deixando o cargo, agradecia e despedia do povo, o que não é bem verdade, porque a carta de renúncia dele não foi aceita. Ele foi retirado por impeachment. E por impeachment, ele não ganha o status de senador vitalício e não ganha imunidade parlamentar. Por isso, logo em seguida, o Ministério Público indiciou o ex-presidente, pediu a prisão dele, e ele está em casa em prisão domiciliar. O vice-presidente assumiu também aqui agora há pouco. Preparamos uma reportagem sobre esse dia frenético", diz o repórter César Menezes.

A sessão que abriu os trabalhos nesta sexta-feira (6) no Senado paraguaio deveria ter começado com a defesa do presidente do país, Santiago Peña. Mas, logo cedo, ele apresentou um pedido de adiamento por 72 horas, alegando que só recebeu a notificação no fim da noite de quinta-feira (5) e não teve tempo suficiente para escolher um advogado de confiança para exercer o direito de defesa.

Por 39 votos a 3, os senadores recusaram o adiamento. E quando a sessão foi retomada, dois advogados de Peña se apresentaram. Eles alegaram que o presidente do país não tem poder sobre as ações denunciadas, referentes à crise financeira do Banco Ueno, e que essas ações são de responsabilidade de outros agentes públicos e privados.

Santiago Peña se tornou o centro de uma crise política depois da quebra do principal banco digital do Paraguai. Na última terça-feira (3), o Banco Central do país interrompeu as atividades do Ueno Bank e a Justiça determinou a prisão de oito diretores. Cerca de 3 milhões de pessoas, incluindo aposentados, ficaram sem acesso ao próprio dinheiro. Quase a metade da população do Paraguai. O fechamento do banco provocou protestos em todo o país.

Até 2025, Santiago Peña era um dos acionistas do grupo controlador do banco. Ele é acusado de conflito de interesses e de favorecer o banco Ueno.

Presidente destituído do Paraguai, Santiago Peña é preso em Assunção — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

Quando a sessão no Senado foi retomada à tarde, a senadora da oposição Yolanda Paredes contestou a legitimidade dos advogados de defesa apresentados de última hora. Na sequência, os senadores do comitê de acusação apresentaram argumentos sobre a responsabilidade de Santiago Peña na quebra do banco. Os advogados fizeram, então, as alegações finais.

Exatamente às 18h, o Senado abriu a quinta e última sessão extraordinária para concluir o processo de impeachment. Depois de uma hora de discursos, foi feita a votação. E o resultado foi unânime: 44 a 0. Santiago Peña foi destituído da presidência do Paraguai.

Do lado de fora, um forte esquema de segurança foi montado para evitar tumulto durante manifestações da população em frente ao Congresso. Nesta sexta-feira (6), a porta de uma das agências em Assunção amanheceu coberta por cartazes de protesto.

O comando do país, agora, fica nas mãos do vice, Pedro Alliana. Ele não foi incluído no processo de impeachment e assumiu como presidente interino. Alliana também é do Partido Colorado. Formado em relações internacionais, tem 52 anos, e já foi deputado e governador.

articles.title: Caso Richarlison: Governo suspende registros de Willer Tomaz em Angra | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a Secretaria de Patrimônio da União, responsável por gerir os imóveis do governo federal, a suspensão visa restringir possíveis transferências de posse dos imóveis.
articles.summary: A Secretaria de Patrimônio da União bloqueou a transferência de quatro imóveis de Willer Tomaz, incluindo a área de R$ 10 milhões reivindicada pelo jogador Richarlison.
articles.body:
A Secretaria de Patrimônio da União, órgão do Ministério de Gestão e Inovação em Serviços Públicos responsável por gerir os imóveis do governo federal, suspendeu os registros de quatro imóveis do advogado Willer Tomaz Ilha Comprida, em Angra dos Reis (RJ).

Os quatro imóveis estão localizados na Ilha Comprida. Um desses imóveis é o que foi reivindicado pelo jogador de futebol Richarlison. A medida atende a uma representação administrativa da deputada federal Tábata Amaral (PSB-SP).

O caso chamou atenção especialmente durante as eleições, quando o atacante do Tottenham acusou o senador e então candidato à Presidência da República Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) de envolvimento na disputa por conta da sua amizade com Willer Tomaz.

Segundo a SPU, “a suspensão temporária visa restringir eventuais transferências de posse dos imóveis da União nos quais as edificações foram construídas”.

Em nota, a defesa de Willer Tomaz afirmou que ele e a WT Administração não foram notificados e nem intimados de qualquer procedimento e que a transferência foi aprovada pela SPU, reconhecida e confirmada pela Justiça.

"A transferência foi aprovada pela SPU/RJ, reconhecida como válida repetidas vezes e confirmada pela Justiça em decisão transitada em julgado. O jogador Richarlison, que admitiu ter comprado o terreno de invasores, renunciou no processo a qualquer direito sobre o imóvel. Não há disputa nem irregularidade".

O órgão apura irregularidades no processo que autorizou Willer Tomaz a ocupar o terreno em Ilha Comprida. Um dos pontos é o registro que mostra que a autorização para a transferência dos direitos ao advogado foi emitida sem verificação de regularidade quanto às obrigações do ocupante perante a União.

A solicitação para ocupação teria sido feita às 11h e 33min do dia 11 de julho 2022 e autorizada às 13h e 13min, menos de 2 horas depois.

A disputa começou em 2020, quando Richarlison afirma ter investido R$ 10 milhões na compra da mansão, por meio de uma empresa da qual é sócio. Segundo o jogador, Flávio Bolsonaro demonstrou interesse na propriedade, mas ele se recusou a vendê-la.

O atacante acusa o senador de ter se aliado ao advogado Willer Tomaz, amigo de Flávio, para tirar dele os direitos sobre o imóvel.

Flávio Bolsonaro nega envolvimento na disputa, embora tenha visitado a propriedade e sido incluído como testemunha no processo judicial sobre a posse da casa.

Willer Tomaz afirma que sua empresa adquiriu legalmente os direitos de ocupação da ilha e de um imóvel no local.

Segundo nota enviada pelo advogado, Richarlison negociou com posseiros que não eram os legítimos proprietários. Ele também sustenta que a empresa ligada ao jogador sofreu derrotas na Justiça, inclusive no Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ).

O g1 mostrou que o advogado tem outras cinco casas em ilhas de Angra dos Reis, na Costa Verde do Rio de Janeiro, além da que virou alvo de disputa com o jogador Richarlison.

Com exceção de uma, as casas foram compradas entre 2021 e 2022, na mesma época em que Flávio apresentou ao Senado Federal um projeto de lei para estimular empreendimentos em Angra, permitindo a municipalização das unidades de conservação federais e estaduais.

Também no mesmo período, Flávio foi o relator da PEC das Praias no Senado. O texto propõe permitir a privatização das ilhas marítimas do país, hoje pertencentes à União. Os dois projetos continuam em tramitação.

Os planos para a Costa Verde do Rio vêm desde o governo de Jair Bolsonaro. Em maio de 2019, o então presidente afirmou que queria fazer de Angra "uma nova Cancún".

As casas compradas por empresas de Willer Tomaz em Angra são localizadas na:

Ilha Comprida: em um terreno de 175,2 mil m² , comprada pela empresa WT Administração de Imóveis e Bens, em setembro de 2021. Valor patrimonial registrado de R$ 5,7 milhões;

Ilha Comprida: em um terreno de 32,8 mil m² , comprada pela empresa WT Administração de Imóveis e Bens, em setembro de 2021. Valor patrimonial registrado de R$ 2,1 milhões;

Ilha Comprida: em um terreno de 181,8 mil m² , comprada pela empresa WT Administração de Imóveis e Bens, em setembro de 2021. Valor patrimonial registrado de R$ 6 milhões;

Ilha Comprida: em um terreno de 2,1 mil m² , comprada pela empresa WT Administração de Imóveis e Bens, em julho de 2022. Valor patrimonial registrado de R$ 2,9 milhões (imóvel disputado com Richarlison);

Ilha do José André: em um terreno de 57,3 mil m² , comprada pela empresa Friponor Brasil Turismo, Empreendimentos e Participações, em 2008. Valor patrimonial registrado de R$ 23,7 milhões.

Os dados são de um levantamento feito nos sistemas da SPU e em registros de cartório.

Tomaz é dono, também, de cotas de uma sexta casa em Angra, na Ilha do Jorge, registrada em nome da empresa Real Estate Duo 4, pertencente ao grupo Prime You.

articles.title: US judge temporarily blocks Trump’s Washington arch
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - A judge temporarily blocked construction from beginning on President Donald Trump's proposed 250-foot (76-meter) triumphal arch...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - A judge temporarily blocked construction from beginning on President Donald Trump's proposed 250-foot (76-meter) triumphal arch in Washington late on Thursday, shortly after it won a key approval.

US District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a 14-day ‌restraining order following the National Capital Planning Commission 8-4 vote to approve the project after it heard from about 100 opponents, ‌including Democratic lawmakers.

The Trump administration contends Congress approved the arch more than 100 years ago when it also authorized construction of a bridge across the Potomac River.

"The sheer improbability that ​a 100-year-old statute would contain authority, unknown to every previous administration, to erect a 250-foot arch at a principal location in the nation's capital indicates how far (the government) must stretch to justify this project," Chutkan wrote.

She said approval would result in construction for about three years "that will disrupt traffic, create noise, result in large-scale excavation, and more."

The Justice Department had said earlier that if the project had been approved it expected an initial six to ‌eight months of construction focused on excavation and foundation ⁠work could begin as soon as Thursday. Above-ground construction would start in May 2027 at the earliest, with the job expected to take 33 to 39 months total.

"It will snarl traffic for years, impact the nearby airport, ⁠and present even more serious threats to public safety that this commission has refused to acknowledge and grapple with," said Representative Don Beyer, a Democrat who represents northern Virginia.

The National Park Service also said late on Thursday it had approved the project.

The arch is among several costly projects Trump is pushing in Washington ​despite ​opposition from local officials and conservationists. They include rebuilding the Reflecting Pool at ​the Lincoln Memorial, constructing a massive White House ballroom and ‌overhauling the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

The arch has faced significant opposition in the courts. The state of Virginia and the District of Columbia sued the National Park Service and the Department of the Interior on Saturday, seeking to halt the start of construction, calling it "legally indefensible" and arguing that Congress has not approved it.

They also raised a number of concerns about the project's impact on traffic

At an event on Monday to highlight improvements to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, Trump said the arch would also serve as a military asset and would be able ‌to house drones and snipers.

"It's right smack in the middle of everything, so very ​important for our military. But from a beautification standpoint, it'll be the most beautiful ​arch in the world," Trump said.

The arch, which would include an ​eternal flame and floodlights to make it visible to pilots, would be situated across the Potomac River from ‌the Lincoln Memorial on a highway roundabout near the entrance ​to Arlington National Cemetery.

It would resemble ​the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, but stand more than 80 feet taller. It would also be nearly as tall as the US Capitol, which at 288 feet, can be seen across much of Washington. The site is near airplanes' final approach to Ronald ​Reagan Washington National Airport.

A rendering showed the flame ‌would be held by a 60-foot-tall gold, winged female figure positioned atop the arch and flanked by gold flying eagles.

Critics say ​it would place some graves at Arlington National Cemetery in shadow, while the Trump administration said it would honor veterans.

(Reporting ​by David Shepardson; Editing by Chris Sanders, Edmund Klamann and Raju Gopalakrishnan)

articles.title: GOP’s losses will raise pressure on conservative Supreme Court justices to retire
articles.summary: The GOP’s sweeping losses in the midterm elections Tuesday set up an unsettling possibility for the party: If it doesn’t act now to confirm a new Supreme Cou...
articles.body:
The GOP's sweeping losses in the midterm elections Tuesday set up an unsettling possibility for the party: If it doesn't act now to confirm a new Supreme Court justice, it may not have another chance for years to come.

That prospect is likely to ramp up pressure on the court's two oldest conservatives - Justices Samuel A. Alito Jr., 76, and Clarence Thomas, 78 - to retire during the lame-duck period, while Republicans still have the votes to get a nominee confirmed by the Senate. The new Senate, in which Democrats will hold a majority, is seated on Jan. 3.

Alito, who joined the court in 2006, said last month he has no plans to retire during the lame-duck session. Thomas has said in the past he has no plans to step down from the court. He joined the court in 1991 and could become the longest-serving justice in its history in 2028.

But given the magnitude of Democratic inroads in the Senate, legal and political experts said it could be 2033 before Republicans have a realistic shot at winning back enough seats in that chamber to approve a conservative justice.

At that point, Alito and Thomas would be well into their 80s. Neither responded to a request for comment.

"I think both have been making an implicit bet that they will live long enough … so that a Republican president can replace them with someone ideologically similar," said Ed Whelan, a conservative attorney and senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center.

This is likely to make many Republicans antsy, particularly those mindful of the lesson of Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, who died while still on the bench at 87, in September 2020.

The liberal justice's death allowed Republicans to move the court in a more conservative direction when they confirmed Justice Amy Coney Barrett to replace her weeks later. President Donald Trump nominated Barrett to replace Ginsburg, and over the vociferous objections of Democrats, Senate Republicans quickly muscled the nomination through just ahead of the 2020 presidential election.

Trump remade the court with three picks in his first term - Barrett, Neil M. Gorsuch and Brett M. Kavanaugh - who pushed the court sharply to the right.

The Supreme Court's conservative 6-3 supermajority has delivered historic opinions on abortion, affirmative action, religious rights and much more that have thrilled Republicans. A younger replacement for Alito or Thomas could lock that advantage in for years to come.

Liberals accused Republicans of hypocrisy for rapidly confirming Barrett after they blocked President Barack Obama's nomination of Merrick Garland for 11 months in 2016, saying it was too close to the presidential election to confirm him. Trump won the White House, and Garland's nomination was scuttled.

Some observers think the window has already closed for Trump to nominate a fourth justice, which would allow him to leave a mark on the Supreme Court that few presidents have enjoyed.

Republicans control 53 seats in the upper chamber, compared with 47 held by Democrats. But that split will shift to 52-48 as soon as Dec. 15, when Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) is seated as a result of a special election. A handful of moderate Senate Republicans like Maine's Susan Collins and Alaska's Lisa Murkowski might also have to be persuaded to back a Trump pick.

The margin of error is thin enough that Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) posted Tuesday night on X that Trump probably won't be able to get a suitable nominee confirmed.

"Chance of confirming a worthy successor to Justice Thomas and/or Alito during President Trump's term: Zero," DeSantis wrote. "Chance of confirming a worthy successor during a hypothetical GOP admin 2029-2033: probably zero (GOP won't be able to recapture enough seats in 28)."

Harry Litman, a law professor at UCLA and a former U.S. attorney, said the optics of a justice retiring during the lame-duck session would also tarnish his or her reputation.

"It would be the most crass and nakedly political resignation in the court's history," Litman said.

Emily Hampsten, a spokeswoman for Sen. Dick Durbin (Illinois), the Democratic whip and a member of the Judiciary Committee, said a lame-duck nominee would create a backlash among voters and Democrats.

"The American people will hold them accountable in 2028, and Democrats could justifiably refuse to confirm any Trump nominees for the next two years," Hampsten said.

That would curtail one of Trump's other biggest legacies - the nomination of hundreds of lower court federal judges.

Steve Vladeck, a Georgetown law professor, wrote on his blog that a lame-duck confirmation fight might also backfire on the GOP by building support for court reforms that Democrats are already eyeing during the next Congress.

"The question would no longer be whether the Court deserves to be restructured, but whether the other side has left Democrats any choice," Vladeck wrote.

Gabe Roth, executive director of the reform group Fix the Court, said he thinks only small reforms will be possible while Trump is still president over the next two years.

"Democrats would do well to focus on areas within the realm of court reform where there's already strong bipartisan support," Roth said. "That includes banning stock trading in the federal courts, adding more lower court judgeships to relieve ballooning caseloads, improving workplace conduct protections for judiciary staff and making access to court records free."

Speculation over whether Alito would retire flared over the summer when NPR published an erroneous account saying he was planning on stepping down. The story was later retracted.

Alito said during a round of interviews to promote his new book last month that he had no plans to retire during the current term, which will end in June or July. The justice said he has more to contribute to the court but did consider whether to continue each term.

"I intend to stick around through this term," Alito said in the interview before the Supreme Court's new term began last month. "I made that decision many months ago."

articles.title: Young men backed Trump in 2024. The midterms show they’re swing voters
articles.summary: Young men backed Democrats by 25 points in the midterms just two years after helping Trump win the White House.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Democrats won a resounding midterm victory with help from a group that swung toward Republicans just two years ago: young men.

Men ages 18 to 29 backed Democratic House candidates by 25 points, according to estimates from The New York Times . That's a 39-point swing from 2024, when Donald Trump won young men by 14 points.

Young men's shift toward Democrats was more than double the 18-point change among men overall.

The results complicate the narrative that emerged after the 2024 election, when podcasters and social media influencers were credited with driving a Republican "vibe shift" among young men.

"The Manosphere Won," WIRED magazine declared in November 2024. The Washington Post attributed Trump's victory , in part, to his appeal in "testosterone-fueled corners of the internet."

Trump's success raised questions about a durable conservative realignment among Gen Z men, but even at the time, there was little evidence their policy views or social attitudes had changed much.

Instead, young men have shown they're swing voters who want action, not blame, argues Richard Reeves, president of the American Institute for Boys and Men .

"Men didn't become Republicans in 2024, and they didn't just become Democrats last night," Reeves wrote after this week's midterms.

Daniel Cox, director of the Survey Center on American Life, noted in a post on X that half of young men who identified as moderate and a quarter who identified as liberal backed Trump in 2024.

That flipped this year, with 59% of moderate young men and nearly 20% of conservatives backing Democrats, Cox pointed out.

"The last presidential election was not an ideological realignment; it was deep disaffection with an unpopular administration," Cox wrote Wednesday .

Now, it's the Trump administration that's unpopular

Most male midterm voters (59%) disapproved of Trump's job performance, according to NBC News exit polling.

A plurality (38%) ranked the economy as the country's top issue, and nearly two-thirds said the president's policies had worsened economic conditions.

Voters ages 18 to 29 were even more likely than men overall to say the economy was their top issue and that Trump's policies had made it worse.

"Both parties need to compete for the votes of men, especially young men, if they are to succeed in 2028," Reeves wrote.

articles.title: South Florida candidate sues election official, alleging bias in a contentious, razor-thin race
articles.summary: MIAMI — South Florida Democratic congressional candidate Eliott Rodriguez filed a federal lawsuit against the Miami-Dade supervisor of elections Friday, citi...
articles.body:
MIAMI — South Florida Democratic congressional candidate Eliott Rodriguez filed a federal lawsuit against the Miami-Dade supervisor of elections Friday, citing bias after she declined to recuse herself from the recount process. Incumbent Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar is named in the lawsuit as well.

The lawsuit seeks to bar Miami-Dade supervisor of elections, Alina García, from acting as a deciding member of the county canvassing board for the 27th Congressional District, where the results are razor-thin.

Salazar was leading Rodriguez by 1,103 votes or 0.44 percentage points as of Thursday evening. Florida law requires automatic recounts when there is less than a 0.5-point margin. The canvassing board oversees the recount.

Rodriguez's campaign demanded Thursday that García recuse herself from oversight of the recount.

The Rodriguez campaign alleged the attorney representing Salazar in the recount, Robert Fernández, is García's son-in-law and requested immediate confirmation, saying the relationship would raise additional serious concerns, according to the complaint.

The campaign also cited in the lawsuit an interview García gave to The Miami Herald on election night stating, "Maria Elvira is the winner, with or without a recount" and that it was "possible but not probable" there were enough remaining ballots to flip the results.

She added that recounts almost never end up going the other way. "Usually the trend we see is what continues," García was quoted as saying. In other words, if Salazar is ahead, it will likely remain that way.

The Miami Herald also reported that Oren Rosenthal, general counsel for the supervisor of elections, estimated he's seen about 20 recounts, and with the margin that Salazar was leading by on Tuesday night, he said it was unlikely the result will be overturned.

In a press release, García stated, "I want to reiterate that I was elected by the people to perform the duties of the Supervisor of Elections. Nothing disqualifies me form performing those duties including serving on the Canvassing Board. Accordingly, as I have stated previously, I have not recused myself, nor will I."

Juan-Carlos Planas, general counsel for the Miami-Dade Democratic Executive Committee, ran against García in the 2024 supervisor of elections race.

"If candidates are going to hire relatives from the supervisor of elections, we're going down a very dangerous precedent," he said. "Can you imagine going into court and litigants are hiring relatives of the judge? The judge would be removed from office."

On Thursday evening, the day before the final counting of ballots and certification of results was scheduled to take place, an attorney representing Rodriguez sent a letter to García demanding she step away from matters involving the race.

"This goes beyond any ethical standards. The canvassing board is a quasi-judicial body so she sits as a quasi-judicial official," Planas said. "This is a quasi-judicial body and therefore she should recuse herself like any other judge would."

García, a Republican who served one term in the Florida state House before winning the election for supervisor of elections in 2024, has posed in pictures with fellow Republican leaders, including Salazar and President Donald Trump . She is the first elected supervisor of elections. It was previously a nonpartisan position appointed by the county's mayor.

Few pundits considered the race competitive this time around, but the district shifted 14.26 points toward Democrats compared with the 2024 presidential election.

Salazar's office did not respond to a request for comment.

"My opponent is behaving like an election denier, attempting to turn this process into a political circus because he does not like election outcome," Salazar posted on X Thursday night.

Salazar and Rodriguez are both Cuban American and former journalists. Salazár has won three consecutive terms to represent the heavily Hispanic 27th Congressional District. She and Trump comfortably won the district in 2024.

There were signs of trouble for Salazar in September when she released an ad where she broke with Trump on his immigration policies.

"Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," she said in the ad while standing in front of the White House.

Her district has been particularly impacted by Trump's harsh immigration enforcement, including a record number of deportations of Cubans. While Trump criticized Salazar after the ad, he eventually endorsed her before Election Day.

articles.title: Democrats' midterm gains complicate path forward on permitting bill
articles.summary: (The Center Square) – Despite broad bipartisan support of the U. S.
articles.body:
(The Center Square) – Despite broad bipartisan support of the U.S. Senate's permitting reform bill, which aims to expedite energy projects and lower electricity costs, Democratic leadership in the House is now demanding more concessions.

Senate leaders were hoping to hold a vote on the long-awaited Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act during the upcoming lame-duck session, the last eight weeks of the 119th Congress.

The primary purpose of the 417-page bill is to expedite the permitting approval process for energy-related projects – such as natural gas pipelines, drilling and mining, and data center infrastructure – primarily by scaling back environmental and judicial reviews.

Permitting-associated expenses cost manufacturers a cumulative $12.1 billion per year, according to the National Association of Manufacturers. By expediting the timelines that contribute to higher permitting costs, the BAAJA would cut that number by 35%, saving manufacturers $4.2 billion per year, NAM says.

Supporters of BAAJA say it will increase energy supply, reduce Americans' electric bills, and create more jobs as the country enters a new era of energy demand.

Monumental election wins, however, have galvanized some Democrats to push for changes, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is set to become House speaker in January.

Jeffries said the bill "falls short in several areas," specifically naming environmental and tribal protections in his post-election comments to Politico.

Jeffries' remarks echo the concerns of BAAJA-critical organizations, who argue the bill in its current form would trample state and community rights by limiting litigation and local input, erode environmental safeguards, and make it more difficult for states and tribes to oppose federal projects and data centers.

Rep. Jared Huffman, D-Calif., wants lawmakers to hold a hearing on the bill and allow amendments to be introduced before holding a vote.

"House Democrats support, and will deliver, responsible permitting reform. But as Speaker-elect Jeffries said today, and as some of us have said for weeks, we must have a chance to fix the most glaring flaws in BAAJA," Huffman posted Thursday on social media.

But with Democrats having campaigned largely on affordability promises, some view the results as even more of a reason to pass legislation targeting energy costs as soon as possible, rather than make ultimatums.

"Modernizing our permitting process is an important way to lower utility costs, create good-paying local jobs, and secure our energy future, and we need to get it done," Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kan., said in a statement Friday explicitly breaking with Jeffries.

"Standing up for working families means getting this done the right way and ensuring we don't repeat mistakes of the past," Davids added. "I am working with House and Senate leaders in both parties to fix these provisions so we can pass a bill that lowers everyday costs, respects Tribal nations, and protects our environment."

Without faster buildout of high-voltage transmission lines, additional power generation facilities, and other energy infrastructure, the U.S. demand for energy will overtake supply within the next ten years, according to the North American Electric Reliability Corporation.

articles.title: Three Justice Department officials resign following midterms
articles.summary: Three Justice Department officials have now resigned in the wake of a tidal wave of Democratic midterm election wins.
articles.body:
Jason Reding Quiñones, the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida, the prosecutorial office that has been running a probe dubbed the "grand conspiracy" investigation into people who investigated President Donald Trump , said in a social media post that he submitted his resignation Friday, Nov. 6.

Reding Quiñones wasn't alone in exiting Friday. John Eisenberg, the assistant attorney general leading the DOJ's National Security Division, is also leaving the department, Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed on social media .

Huge banner of Trump unveiled on Justice Department HQ

The pair follow in the footsteps of another departing official, DOJ Civil Rights Division head Harmeet Dhillon . Her resignation was announced Nov. 5. Dhillon said in a text message to USA TODAY that "these jobs are tough" and had informed Blanche in her resignation letter that she'd "accomplished what I came to do."

It's unclear what the shakeup could mean for the department's work.

A department spokesperson told USA TODAY the DOJ's mission hasn't changed since the midterms, and it is focused on enforcing the law, combatting crime and protecting Americans. The spokesperson said officials who have recently announced they are leaving helped make the country safer and the DOJ was lucky to have them.

The spokesperson didn't respond to USA TODAY's request for comment on whether officials beyond Dhillon, Eisenberg and Reding Quiñones have also departed this week.

DOJ may face heightened scrutiny from Democrat-controlled Congress

Following Democrats' electoral wins this week, the department may face heightened scrutiny next year from Democrat-controlled congressional committees.

Already, Democrats have decried what they say are politically motivated investigations, including the "grand conspiracy" probe and three separate criminal cases against former FBI Director James Comey, a prominent critic of the president. One of those cases was dismissed in November 2025, and the two others remain pending.

The current DOJ has also faced numerous failures to secure indictments from grand juries, even though federal prosecutors' requests for grand jury indictments are typically almost always successful. Late last month, a grand jury refused to indict Cassidy Hutchinson , a former Trump White House aide who implicated Trump in potential wrongdoing during testimony about the Jan. 6, 2021 riot by Trump supporters at the U.S. Capitol.

"LAWYER UP," Rep. Robert Garcia, D–California, who is currently the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, posted on social media Nov. 3, after midterm election results began coming in.

Reding Quiñones isn't the only official tied to the "grand conspiracy" investigation to have left. Joseph diGenova , a former Reagan DOJ official who assisted Trump's efforts to challenge the results of the 2020 presidential election, resigned ahead of the midterms in September, just months after he joined the DOJ to work on the probe. DiGenova later suggested to The New York Post that he was improperly pressured to bring charges.

"If you want indictments where there's no evidence, you have an ethical problem," he said.

The division led by Eisenberg secured a guilty plea from John Bolton , a former Trump national security adviser who became a prominent Trump critic, in a criminal case over Bolton's handling of classified information. Bolton's sentencing is upcoming.

Dhillon dramatically reshaped the DOJ's Civil Rights Division, dropping lawsuits accusing police departments of civil rights violations and directing investigations into potential racial preferences in employment and university admissions , religious liberty issues and local limits on gun ownership . She said on a Breitbart News podcast that, as of August 2025, about 300 of the division's 400 lawyers had left since Trump retook office.

The three DOJ leaders aren't the only Trump officials to exit top roles this week. White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles announced in a social media post Friday that she is leaving her position as well.

Contributing: Francesca Chambers, USA TODAY

articles.title: White House Warns Conservative Groups It Is 'Monitoring' What They Say Amid Discontent Over Midterm Results
articles.summary: The White House insists that the memo isn’t a threat—but given Trump’s history, it’s hard to take that at face value.
articles.body:
With President Donald Trump's unpopularity front and center after Democrats' sweeping midterm victory, Republicans are beginning to criticize the president and his policies.

On Wednesday, Vice President J.D. Vance called out Trump's war of choice in Iran as the "real reason" for why the GOP lost the election. Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis has spent the last few days dissecting voter dissatisfaction, which he told The Sage Steele Show includes the crony capitalism of the "Republicans in Washington." With the GOP seemingly fracturing, the White House is taking steps to rein in potential fallout within the base.

On Thursday, the White House Office of Public Liaison sent a memo to over 3,000 conservative organizations, which The Wall Street Journal reports , "laid out a list of Trump's accomplishments in office and pledged to prevent newly ascendant Democrats from reversing them." The memo ended with one sentence, highlighted in yellow: "As always, we are monitoring statements, press releases, and media engagements from your organizations."​

When the Journal asked for comment, a White House spokeswoman said the memo "wasn't a threat and was part of a larger effort to mobilize outside supporters," insisting that the Office of Public Liaison has sent out similar messages in the past. The Journal didn't find similar language in a review of previous emails from the liaison's office to groups encouraging organizations' advocacy for the president.

It's certainly possible that the liaison office did not intend to threaten conservative groups—it is, after all, the job of the office to monitor what allied groups are doing. However, given the administration's history of tracking and threatening its critics for constitutionally protected speech, the line doesn't exactly read as a friendly reminder.​

In September, for example, Trump banned several major news outlets from the White House, displeased with their negative reporting. "The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS." He stated on Truth Social. "It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!"​ A district court judge blocked the ban in October, finding that Trump's own words showed "unlawful viewpoint discrimination."

The Trump administration has also targeted legal residents for their political speech. Last year, Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested Mahmoud Khalil, a Columbia graduate student, over his role in pro-Palestine campus protests. Khalil was never charged with a crime. Still, the administration deemed he was "subject to removal" because his "presence or activities…would have potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences for the United States."

Trump isn't the first president to crack down on disfavored speech. During the COVID-19 pandemic, former President Joe Biden spent much of his time pressuring social media companies to remove content they deemed "misinformation." Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said that Biden administration officials "repeatedly pressured our teams for months to censor certain COVID-19 content, including humor and satire."

If the Trump White House is threatening these groups, it's unclear what the consequences of disobeying might be. But one thing is for sure: With the president's popularity in doubt after the midterms, a memo reminding allies they're being watched suggests the White House fears its grip on the GOP is slipping.

articles.title: The Hitchhiker’s Guide to what happens next on Capitol Hill
articles.summary: Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan are vying for top House Republican, and incoming progressives challenge Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries for leadership.
articles.body: The midterms are over. But even more pitched battles are underway. These are internal House and Senate leadership elections. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., won’t pursue the minority leader post. President Trump doesn’t always see eye-to-eye with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., but the president hasn’t demanded a change there. Some incoming House and Senate progressives have expressed their reservations about House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., despite the stunning Democratic wins from Tuesday night. REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: A DEMOCRATIC MAJORITY COULD EXPOSE THE LIMITS OF THE PROGRESSIVE AGENDA Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., has long warned he might not support Schumer for Majority Leader. "If you’re Chuck Schumer, I’m dangerous," El-Sayed advised in late June. The Michigan Democrat ducked the question when asked about supporting Schumer on NBC just after the election. "I am going to vote for the option that gives me the best chance of getting money out of politics. Putting money in pockets and passing Medicare for all," said El-Sayed. "I'm interested to see, working with the rest of our caucus, what options we've got." By Thursday on CNN, El-Sayed was reiterating his support for Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who hasn’t announced he’s running for anything. "I think he'd be an amazing Senate majority leader," said El-Sayed of Van Hollen. But even other newcomers weren’t committing to Schumer. "No, I will not (support Schumer)," Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, D-Kan., said on Fox before the election. "And I've already said I'm not going to vote (for him)." "I think it's really clear that both parties are ready for a new generation of leadership," Sen.-elect Annie Andrews, D-S.C., told colleague Bret Baier. "I told Sen. Schumer that I'm going to support somebody else," offered Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, D-Maine. But Schumer is shrugging that off. "I'll be re-elected as majority leader," Schumer said when asked by reporters on Wednesday. "But the issue is focusing on the American people and what they want." Schumer only needs around 29 of his members to support him in a secret caucus vote to become majority leader. That’s a majority of expected Senate Democrats who will serve next year. At least five members of the Democratic Socialists of America are pledging to withhold their support for Jeffries as the first Black House speaker in U.S. history unless they secure commitments for their agenda. The successful candidate for speaker requires an outright majority of the entire House — 218 votes of 435, if all Representatives-elect cast ballots — when the new Congress convenes Jan. 3. Keep in mind that House Democrats may score more than 260 seats once all races are settled. So, he can afford dozens of defections. For House Republicans, Johnson may have signaled his future last month when speaking to colleague Aishah Hasnie. "If God moves on our hearts and says we should go back to my hometown of Shreveport and start a lawn business, I'll do that," said Johnson. Now it’s far from certain that Johnson will soon channel Groundskeeper Willie from the Simpsons. But perhaps becoming "The Lawnmower Man" is a better option for Johnson than getting mowed down by your own colleagues in a bid for minority leader. Maybe the grass IS greener back in Louisiana. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., and Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, are running to become the House’s top Republican. House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., wants to return as minority whip. He’s facing a challenge from Rep. August Pfluger, R-Texas. But here’s the trick. How do these House Republicans win the leadership positions yet maintain their own coalitions? It’s unclear if Republicans think that Jordan and Scalise are right for the party — right now. Both are aligned with President Trump. And some Republicans hope to move past that. Regardless, Democrats campaigned on two things: the cost of living and holding the Trump administration accountable. But what does the Democrats’ legislative agenda look like? This isn’t like 1994, when former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, R-Ga., famously crafted the 10-point Contract with America as a pledge to voters as to what Republicans would do if they flipped the House for the first time in 40 years. CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER' Democrats have a host of ideas on what they plan to vote on. "We have to first get in there and really focus on rolling back the cuts from the one big ugly bill," Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton, D-Ill., promised on CNN. Also expect votes on renewing expired Obamacare subsidies. Democrats demanded money to offset the costs of rising premiums in exchange for their votes to fund the government. The House finally passed a bill to do that. But the Senate didn’t. The standoff over the Obamacare aid was the key component to last year’s record-breaking, 43-day government shutdown. "The shutdown sharpened the American people's view of the distinction between the parties on this crucial issue," Schumer said. Democrats are also focused on a key issue from the midterms: the future of AI and data centers. They’re concerned that AI threatens American jobs. "This revolt against data centers are just the initial tremors of a bigger AI earthquake that is upending American politics," said Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, chairman of the Progressive Caucus. "And we have to be on the right side of this issue." There will undoubtedly be votes to end the war in Iran — perhaps by cutting off money for those operations. The House approved three "war powers" resolutions. The Senate green-lighted one. But those machinations did nothing to hem in the president on the war. Democrats believe that ending the war will reduce gas prices. And that, in turn, will lower the cost of groceries. Congressional Republicans balked at unwinding tariffs imposed by President Trump. So, there could be votes on that front, too. Democrats believe the election shifted the dynamic of Republicans aligning behind the President in near lockstep. "This is the time for (Republicans) to show the courage to end this irrational and self-defeating tariff regime that Trump has put in place," said Rep. Greg Stanton, D-Ariz. "Most of them realize that the tariffs from a fiscal and economic perspective are completely self-defeating." However, some Republicans aren’t ready to abandon the old playbook, clinging to the GOP’s hallmark legislative achievement of this Congress. "I think the tax cuts and the Big, Beautiful Bill were underappreciated by the electorate," Rep. Chris Smith, R-N.J., proffered. President Trump signaled he’ll both work with Democrats and deploy his veto pen. But it’s about the math. When all House races are settled, Democrats could control more than 260 House seats. That’s astonishing. They’re guaranteed 54 Senate seats with Mississippi and Alaska still undecided It’s about the math. Overriding a veto requires two-thirds of both bodies. That’s 290 in the House and 67 in the Senate. If Democrats hover around 260 seats in the House — and Republicans are ready to ditch the president — hitting the 290 mark isn’t out of reach. If Democrats clock in at 56 seats in the Senate, cobbling together 11 GOP votes to reach 67 might be tougher. Especially with GOP Trump antagonists like former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and senators John Cornyn, R-Texas; Bill Cassidy, R-La.; and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., departing. But they’re in range. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP It all hinges on what Democrats can pass. And what the president is willing to sign.

articles.title: The White House’s post-election shake-up: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, we dive into President Donald Trump’s decision to make a change at chief of staff. Plus, Kristen Welker examines how voters once again rejected the status quo.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, we dive into President Donald Trump’s decision to make a change at chief of staff. Plus, Kristen Welker examines how voters once again rejected the status quo. — Adam Wollner Trump names Stephen Miller his new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles By Jonathan Allen and Rebecca Shabad President Donald Trump has turned to MAGA favorite Stephen Miller to lead the White House after Republicans got trounced in Tuesday’s midterm elections, losing both chambers of Congress by wide margins. Trump announced the change at the top on Truth Social this afternoon, with Miller, his deputy chief of staff, taking over chief of staff duties from Susie Wiles on Monday. Wiles submitted her resignation Thursday night, according to a White House official. The shift from Wiles, a longtime establishment figure in Florida and national political circles, to Miller, the hard-charging architect of the president’s mass-deportation campaign, sends a signal to a fractured Republican Party that Trump intends to strengthen ties to the MAGA base in his final two years in office. It also portends an even more contentious relationship with Democrats in Congress, who have demonized Miller for years. “Miller knows the key issues and is a true believer — and he knows the ecosystem around the issues,” said Steve Bannon, a former senior Trump aide and host of ‘The War Room” podcast. “Stephen gets parachuted in and takes immediate control.” On a recent phone call with an ally, Trump praised Miller as an aide who gets things done and doesn’t just tell him what he wants to hear. The ally said that Miller will be combative with Congress, particularly when it comes to any investigations Democrats point toward the administration. “When the president says, ‘Do this,’ Stephen will do it, and he’ll leave bodies behind doing it,” the ally said. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is widely expected to become speaker in January, called for Miller to be fired, not promoted. “Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” Jeffries wrote on X. “His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today.” Read more → The midterms reveal a much larger slice of the electorate is up for grabs Analysis by Kristen Welker We thought the 2024 presidential contest was a realignment election, one that would scramble political alliances and change the way both parties try to win for years to come. It turns out that we were only right about the second half. As the dust settles on the 2026 midterms, where Democrats made deep inroads in red states and districts to rack up historic gains in the House and Senate (with more key races still uncalled), one major takeaway is that the group of voters who aren’t strictly guided by pure partisanship is far larger than many may have thought. Those same young, Latino and disaffected voters that helped power President Donald Trump’s victory in 2024 swung dramatically back to Democrats two years later, underscoring that the last two elections weren’t realignments, but rejections of the status quo. After Trump campaigned on tackling rising inflation and bringing down costs, pre-election and exit polling this year makes clear these voters believe he didn’t keep his promises. But just like these swing voters were not permanently a part of the GOP coalition after 2024, Democrats can’t take them for granted now. It now falls to Democrats to figure out how to follow through with the mandate they were given in a divided government, and how to avoid self-inflicted damage from their own factionalism. And Republicans will face a different, yet inextricably linked task — sifting through the wreckage of a disappointing election and figuring out the path forward, not unlike what Democrats faced after 2024. Where both parties go next will shape the lame duck period before the new Congress is sown in, the legislative goals both parties will pursue over the next two years, and, of course, the 2028 presidential election. We’ll sort through all the fallout from the midterms this Sunday on “Meet the Press.” I’ll be joined by Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, D-Kansas, Florida Republican Gov.-elect Byron Donalds, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. Related reads: How Abdul El-Sayed swung young men from Trump by 55 points in Michigan, by Allan SmithMany Republicans leaned into the ‘culture wars’ on the campaign trail. It didn’t work, by Daniel ArkinHow anger helped fuel Latino voter turnout and a historic Democratic shift in Texas, by Suzanne Gamboa and Natasha Korecki That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. articles.title: Why it's still too early to call the US Senate race in Mississippi
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Nearly 2,500 votes separate Democrat Scott Colom and Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the race for U.
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Nearly 2,500 votes separate Democrat Scott Colom and Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the race for U.S. Senate in Mississippi, and votes are still being counted on Friday. Here's why the race is still too early to call.

An unknown number of ballots are outstanding

To call a race, The Associated Press relies on its estimate of how many votes remain to be counted to ensure that the trailing candidate has no path to overtake the leading candidate. The AP calculates this value based on factors including past turnout, population changes, voter registration totals and any early turnout figures provided by elections officials. The estimate of the number of votes that remain to be counted is revised continuously on election night and in the days after.

On Friday morning, the AP's outstanding vote estimate stood at around 44,000 votes in the Mississippi Senate race. After obtaining updated information across the state, the estimate as of 4:45 p.m. ET is now closer to 30,000 votes. However, that figure could change as additional details are gathered.

Many counties in Mississippi — including larger counties like Hinds and Rankin — have historically reported their absentee ballots and provisional ballots after Election Day results have been counted. In the 2024 general election, 12.7% of votes cast were counted after all precincts reported on election night, and the AP's estimates take this into account. In some counties, it is unclear how many — if any — absentee ballots have yet been counted. With little insight into the process, the AP's estimates are largely based on past reporting patterns.

Every state votes differently, and Mississippi's particularities are at play

Most Mississippi voters cast their ballots in person on Election Day. Only a limited number of people vote by absentee ballot, as the state requires voters to provide an excuse for not being able to vote in person.

Mississippi also has some of the strictest voter I.D. laws in the nation. If voters are unable to provide a photo I.D. at the polls, election officials let them complete a provisional ballot — which is only counted if the voter presents their identification to officials within five business days of Election Day. A voter may also have to cast a provisional ballot if their voter registration status is found to be inactive when they arrive at the polls. This can happen if a voter is erroneously believed to have become ineligible to vote when the officials maintain election rolls.

Unlike in some other states, there is no central vote reporting system for the state of Mississippi, and few counties release election results online. Instead, AP journalists and analysts communicate with each of the state's 82 counties directly for the latest available information on vote counts.

Some counties release preliminary absentee vote results on election night, while others release them in the days following the election. In Mississippi, absentee ballots must be postmarked by Election Day and received within five business days of the election, or Nov. 10, to be counted — meaning the number of absentee votes can continue to climb after the election.

Counties are required to report the results of provisional ballots when they report their certified results to the state 10 days after the election on Nov. 13. On Thursday, Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said that about 7,000 provisional ballots had been processed, of which about 80% had been accepted.

The AP is continuously working to gather additional data on the number of outstanding ballots.

As of Friday at 4:45 p.m. ET, the AP estimates that roughly 7% of ballots have yet to be counted in Hinds County, a Democratic stronghold. In 2024, roughly 15% of votes had not been counted yet in Hinds County when all Election Day precincts had reported. The AP did not receive another vote update in the county until the state certified its election. In Hinds, Colom currently has a roughly 47,000-vote lead over Hyde-Smith.

In red Rankin County, where President Donald Trump won 73% of the vote in 2024, the AP currently estimates that around 2,200 votes are outstanding. County officials told the AP on Friday that they have 1,667 provisional ballots, 282 mail ballots received and 138 mail ballots outstanding. It is not clear if all of those votes will be counted. In 2024, roughly 23% of the vote had not been counted yet after all Election Day precincts had reported in Rankin County. The AP received a vote update five days later, bringing the count to 95% of ballots cast, and did not receive the final 5% until the state certified the election.

Mississippi does not have automatic recounts or permit candidates to request a recount. Recounts in the state are held only in the event of a court order.

The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.

Associated Press writers Lauren Johnert in Washington and Hannah Barton in Chicago contributed to this report.

articles.title: FBI agents served an Alaska Senate candidate with a subpoena just days before election day
articles.summary: Gerald Heikes, a longshot candidate, was issued a subpoena as part of a DOJ probe into whether Democrats boosted spoiler candidates.
articles.body:
Days before the midterms, federal prosecutors ordered Gerald Heikes, a longshot Senate hopeful in Alaska, to appear before a grand jury with any records he has related to political groups and other candidates in the race, according to documents reviewed by CNN.

The subpoena was sent as part of an accelerating criminal probe into whether operatives aligned with Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate, sought to recruit spoilers into the race – including another candidate who shares a name with the sitting Republican senator.

Heikes's subpoena, dated one day after a New York Times story alleged Peltola's campaign was linked to that effort, shows prosecutors asking for communications related to the Democrat's campaign as well as several PACs and operatives linked to those groups. The subpoena is signed by a top leader of the civil rights division in Washington, DC, rather than by a prosecutor in Alaska.

"They want me to appear and tell them what I know and how I was recruited, but I wasn't recruited. I just took a chance," Heikes told CNN in an interview on Friday.

The DOJ declined to comment for this story. Peltola has denied any knowledge of efforts to recruit other candidates.

Heikes, a conservative who is now in third place in the still-undecided contest, told CNN that earlier this year an operative whose name he does not know pitched him on running for Senate.

Heikes said he had already been aiming to run for office but decided to run for Senate after that meeting.

"I did it out of fascination… I wanted to see what would happen," Heikes said.

He added, "If they think I'm an operative, they're wrong."

Heikes, a drywall contractor based in Palmer, Alaska, suggested he supports Sen. Sullivan over Peltola, but also said that God initially inspired him to run for office about two decades ago when he sought to be governor. He said his intention has not been to peel votes away from any candidate in the Senate race.

Newly created PACs linked to an out-of-state political operative spent millions of dollars attacking Sen. Sullivan and supporting Heikes, CNN previously reported . Heikes said he knows nothing about who is behind that spending. Heikes has received roughly 2% of the vote in the Senate race, with an estimated quarter of votes outstanding.

Alaska has ranked choice voting , though President Trump posted that votes for Heikes and the other longshot candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., should automatically go to Sen. Sullivan. He referred to Heikes in that post as a "slug."

"I've been called worse. I'm a sheet rocker. I've spent over 40 years in trade, so I know every curse word there is. He's kind of lightweight," Heikes said when asked about that post.

Heikes said FBI agents served him with the subpoena on Saturday, when he was in another part of the state, hours from his home, helping a friend hang drywall.

"They were very polite and then they left," he said.

CNN previously reported that DOJ sent target letters to more than a dozen people it believes helped recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.

The recipients include the leadership of the Elias Law Group, the law firm that represents both the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Peltola's campaign, the sources said.

The subpoena to Heikes demands electronic and paper records related Peltola's campaign and the Elias Law Group, as well as anything related to numerous PACs.

Katelyn Polantz and Hannah Rabinowitz contributed to this report.
