articles.title: 5 surprising facts from the 2026 midterms
articles.summary: Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since George McGill, who was born the year Edison debuted his light bulb.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Democrats won a landslide victory in a midterm election that broke decades-old winning streaks and challenged assumptions about the American electorate .

Here are five facts that show just how unusual this election was.

Kansas hadn't elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932

Democrat Adam Hamilton ended a 94-year losing streak when he defeated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall this week.

The last Democrat Kansas elected to the Senate was George McGill, born in 1879. That's the year Thomas Edison first showed off his light bulb.

Ossoff, Cooper and Talarico would have won without any Election Day votes

Senate races in Georgia, North Carolina and Texas were expected to be competitive.

Instead, the Democratic winners each received more early votes than their Republican opponents received in total, according to state election data reviewed by The Washington Post .

In other words, Jon Ossoff , Roy Cooper and James Talarico would have won their races even if no one had cast a ballot for them on Election Day.

Young men swung 39 points toward Democrats

Men under 30 backed Democratic House candidates by 25 points in the midterms, according to estimates from The New York Times .

That's a 39-point swing from the 2024 presidential election, when Donald Trump won young men by 14 points.

Some of that may come down to who turned out to vote, but it's a sign young men are more up for grabs than many thought just two years ago.

Democrats swept Texas' top statewide offices

James Talarico flipped a U.S. Senate seat and Gina Hinojosa won the governor's race, but the blue wave in Texas didn't stop there.

Democrats won all of the top statewide offices on the ballot, including lieutenant governor, attorney general, comptroller, agriculture commissioner, land commissioner and railroad commissioner.

One of America's bluest states reelected a Republican governor. Again.

Vermont hasn't backed a Republican presidential candidate since 1988 . The governor's office is a different story.

Republican Gov. Phil Scott just won a sixth term, putting him on track to become Vermont's longest-serving governor since it joined the Union.

articles.title: Houston mayor narrows ICE cooperation after midterms: ‘Elections matter’
articles.summary: Houston police will contact immigration authorities only if a person wanted by the feds has been arrested on a jailable charge.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Houston Mayor John Whitmire is narrowing his police department's cooperation with ICE following the rout of Texas Republicans in this week's midterm elections.

Under an executive order the Democrat announced Friday, Houston police will contact federal immigration authorities only if a person wanted by the feds has been arrested on a charge that is subject to jailing.

The nation's fourth-largest city would go after immigrants "that pose a danger, not those that are going about their family business, work and education," Whitmire said. In the case of a traffic incident, "you write a citation or you warn them and they go about their way," he said.

The reversal comes after a deadly ICE-involved shooting in Houston this summer and three days after Democrats swept Texas' statewide offices.

Voters in the traditionally red state ousted Republican Gov. Gregg Abbott, a supporter of President Trump's crackdown on illegal immigration, to elect the state's first Latina executive, Democrat Gina Hinojosa. Voters also overwhelmingly favored Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico over Trump-endorsed Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton for a U.S. Senate seat.

"I've said many times, elections matter," Whitmire said.

Houston and other Texas cities seen as Democratic strongholds have faced pressure from the Abbott administration to cooperate broadly with ICE. The White House has said cities that don't assist federal immigration enforcement are helping to harbor dangerous criminals.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: White House trashes 'peanut-sized brain' Jimmy Kimmel after host demands Trump 'resign'
articles.summary: The White House fired back at Jimmy Kimmel after the ABC late-night host called on President Donald Trump to resign, with spokesman Davis Ingle saying his brain has "rotted."
articles.body: The White House took aim at late-night host Jimmy Kimmel Friday, declaring that his brain has "rotted" after the comedian called on President Donald Trump to "resign." "Jimmy Kimmel’s case of Trump Derangement Syndrome is so advanced that it has completely rotted his peanut-sized brain," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital. "He’s far more entertaining when you’re laughing at him than with him, but unfortunately, his real talent is his failing ratings," Ingle added. "This statement took more brain cells to write than the average Jimmy Kimmel joke." STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE The response followed a string of Trump-focused monologues from Kimmel after the midterm elections, with the ABC host celebrating what he described as a Democratic "blue wave" on Tuesday. During his Wednesday night monologue, Kimmel called on Trump to resign and rejected the president's claim that Republicans would have fared better had he been on the ballot. "That is such crap," Kimmel said. "You were on the ballot. You’re like dog hair. You’re on everything. You’ve infected every nook and cranny of our lives. You divided this country like no one ever divided it before. The only time you ever brought us together was yesterday, when we all teamed up to get rid of you!" Kimmel also referred to the president as "Nappy Gilmore" while showing an imagine of Trump appearing to be asleep during a White House meeting, before urging him to "resign." "Quit already, just quit. Nobody wants you. Even you don’t want to be president anymore. Take that billion dollars’ worth of crypto, buy an island. Maybe Epstein’s island? Wouldn’t that be a perfect end to this story!" Kimmel added. AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI Later in the broadcast, Kimmel addressed a statement Ingle provided to Fox News Digital earlier in the week following the election, in which the spokesman labeled the host a "no-talent loser who has beclowned himself with tanking ratings." That earlier White House statement had added that Kimmel is "so devoid of actual talent that nobody with any commonsense would ever watch him unless it was to laugh at him." "Which is kind of the point of the show, but apparently I’ve beclowned myself once again," Kimmel said, acknowledging the statement on his show and referring to Ingle as "Danny Dingle." "The last thing I want to do is tell you how to do your job, Danny Dingle, but today seems like a bad day for you to call me a loser," the host added. WHITE HOUSE LAUGHS OFF 'BECLOWNED' JIMMY KIMMEL AFTER CRUDE PERSONAL JABS AT NEW PRESS SECRETARY Responding to Kimmel’s post-election coverage earlier in the week, media commentator and Hollywood in Toto editor Christian Toto suggested the host's relationship with ABC could face growing financial pressure. "Jimmy Kimmel long ago traded in comedy for activism. He's a DNC apparatchik, pushing party talking points and occasionally cracking wise along the way. This week's response to the midterms is nothing new," Toto told Fox News Digital Wednesday. "What is new, though, is the tightrope he's walking with ABC. The network wants sizable budget cuts to keep the show afloat. The two sides will likely come up with a compromise, because, for ABC suits, the show's propaganda purposes overshadow financial concerns. But for how long?" Toto added. SETH MEYERS, JOHN OLIVER TELL JIMMY KIMMEL HE'S THEIR 'BULLETPROOF VEST' WHEN IT COMES TO TRUMP CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital’s Hanna Panreck contributed to this report.

articles.title: Multiple top officials exit DOJ after Dems’ midterm wave
articles.summary: The moves leave the department without some of its most seasoned hands just as congressional Democrats gear up for oversight.
articles.body:
Attorney General Todd Blanche is shaking up the Justice Department's senior ranks ahead of an expected clash with Congress and mounting frustration over a string of legal and political failures.

High-profile leaders resigned from the department Thursday and Friday, including Civil Rights Division chief Harmeet Dhillon , National Security Division chief John Eisenberg and U.S. Attorney for Southern Florida Jason Reding Quiñones , who led prosecutors in the so-called "grand conspiracy" case President Donald Trump hoped to mount against his longtime adversaries.

Two people familiar with the personnel changes, granted anonymity to describe internal decision-making, said the departures were not surprising. One person said Blanche had grown frustrated with some of the department's leadership amid struggles to bring high-profile indictments or score big wins in litigation connected to the president's top priorities.

Dhillon, Eisenberg and Reding Quiñones didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

Justice Department spokesperson Kiersten Pels said in a statement the department "was lucky to have had those who have recently announced departures, all of whom contributed to making America safer." Department officials declined to expand on the reason for the departures.

"The Department's mission is unchanged: enforce the law, combat crime, and protect the American people," she said.

Blanche praised Dhillon , Eisenberg and Reding Quiñones in social media posts announcing their resignations.

Henry Whitaker, a counselor to Blanche and veteran of legal battles over executive power, is also leaving DOJ. Patrick Davis, the Justice Department's liaison to Capitol Hill , left the department late last month. Both were expected departures, one of the people said. Whitaker and Davis didn't comment.

The thinning of DOJ's upper ranks leaves the department without some of its most seasoned hands just as congressional Democrats are salivating at the chance to use their newly minted majority to probe the department's most politically sensitive decisions, and the role Trump himself has played in driving them. Democrats have signaled they intend to probe DOJ's controversial settlement in Trump's lawsuit against the IRS over the leaking of his tax returns and "fraudulent and vindictive prosecutions" DOJ brought against Trump's perceived political enemies.

And given their concerns, Trump could struggle to replace Senate-confirmed officials like Dhillon, Reding Quiñones and Eisenberg on a permanent basis. Senate Democrats in January will have the power to delay any confirmation, leaving the department to rely on acting appointees for those jobs.

The Justice Department has suffered a string of high-profile defeats in litigation central to Trump's agenda and personal interests. Courts rejected dozens of lawsuits filed by Dhillon's Civil Rights Division aimed at forcing states to fork over their voter rolls to the federal government — a series of losses that hamstrung the administration's last-ditch effort to impose new ballot security procedures in the waning weeks of the election cycle.

Reding Quiñones' Miami-based office was leading a wide-ranging probe of Trump adversaries the president has accused of improperly targeting him in the investigation of Russian election meddling in the 2016 election.

Despite months of hype and speculation about potentially sweeping indictments, little has come of the effort, and those leading it have largely either left the department or moved on to other priorities.

"It's an incredibly consequential office that's been decimated," said Dan Gelber, a former federal prosecutor who now represents one of the targets of the so-called "grand conspiracy probe," former CIA Director John Brennan. "The most experienced people have fled. The distraction posed by these political investigations has been incredible."

One lawyer in Reding Quiñones' office, granted anonymity to speak candidly, said the office welcomed his exit. "He oversaw a ton of departures, and morale has been super low here. I think the general mood of people here is very happy," the person said.

Former U.S. Attorney for D.C., Joseph diGenova, who worked alongside Reding Quiñones on the politically charged investigation before resigning in September, offered praise for his former colleague.

"Jason Quiñones was one of the finest, most professional, ethical prosecutors I have ever worked with, a genuinely honorable man and I would work with him again," diGenova said Friday.

Eisenberg's office brought a criminal case against former national security adviser John Bolton, who struck a plea deal with prosecutors and pleaded guilty to retaining classified information .

Some of those departing were close to former Attorney General Pam Bondi and all assumed their posts early in her tenure.
authors: Kyle Cheney, Myah Ward, Josh Gerstein and Daniel Lippman

articles.title: Stephen Miller replacing Susie Wiles as chief of staff as Trump grows furious with midterm results, sources say
articles.summary: Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, is departing her role days after catastrophic Republican midterm losses in a seismic staff shakeup at the White...
articles.body:
Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, is departing her role days after catastrophic Republican midterm losses in a seismic staff shakeup at the White House. She will be replaced by Stephen Miller, a longtime aide to President Donald Trump who orchestrated his hardline immigration agenda.

The move is the first major personnel shuffling after the midterms, and came after Trump voiced fury at the strategy that led to Republicans decisively losing majorities in the House and Senate, people familiar with the matter said. And the president signaled Friday it will not be the last, telling CBS News "I do" when asked if he intended to fire people.

"I love my Cabinet. I think they're good. But I'll be doing maybe a few changes. I don't want to mention who," Trump said.

Yet the decision to elevate Miller — one of the most powerful and controversial engineers of Trump's second term — to the top staff position in the West Wing is a sign the president does not intend to fundamentally change his governing approach.

Trump said Wiles would move to his political operation, adding that she "has done an outstanding job." And as he departed the White House for an event in Florida Friday, he praised Miller.

"Stephen's been great, and sometimes in life, you gotta make moves," Trump told reporters shortly after announcing the staffing shakeup.

"Stephen's been with me from beginning. He gets it, very good politically, and he's a very good man," he added.

Wiles submitted her resignation on Thursday evening, two sources familiar with the matter said, and the president announced that the move would take effect Monday.

Trump, who initially appeared unfazed by the results of the Tuesday night midterms, has become angrier as he's watched coverage of the historic losses, according to the people familiar with his response. That sour mood has spread throughout the West Wing, which has become increasingly factionalized in recent days.

Trump made his displeasure with his political team known starting at a tense election night reception in the East Room, according to one of the people familiar with the matter. He vented that deep Republican losses were the result of their strategy. Wiles was among those Trump blamed for the Republican losses, the person said.

As it became clear the president was unhappy with her, Wiles decided to resign, believing he should be able to tap someone to lead his White House that had his confidence, according to a person familiar with her thinking. Wiles had always said she'd remain at the White House until the end of Trump's second term. But the person familiar noted that Wiles had a tough year personally, given her cancer diagnosis and treatment, saying: "It wasn't worth her staying in a job Trump was making clear he didn't want her in."

Since the midterm wipeout, Trump had heard from several allies and associates who urged him to make changes to his senior staff in response to the losses, a source familiar with the matter said. But the move nonetheless came as a shock to many in the administration, and multiple White House officials told CNN it left them concerned about the rest of Trump's second term.

"Susie keeps the trains running on time. I don't know what this looks like moving forward," one official said.

Another Trump ally called it a "catastrophic loss" for the president.

Miller, currently a deputy chief of staff who has been the mastermind behind some of Trump's most polarizing priorities, has widened his portfolio over the past year to include wide swaths of domestic policy and has advocated for an expansive view of executive power. He has worked for Trump since his first presidential campaign, which began in 2015, and has long been viewed as one of Trump's most influential advisers.

His wife, Katie, has a podcast where administration officials and Trump allies regularly appear, and one guest said that some feared they couldn't say no to her requests to be a guest, for fear of getting in Miller's crosshairs.

"It has been the privilege of my lifetime to have served on his team from Day One, and I am honored beyond words to serve as his White House Chief of Staff," Miller posted on X Friday.

He thanked Wiles for her service and friendship before adding, "The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic."

Administration officials who spoke with CNN viewed the change as a sign the White House was doubling down on the president's immigration crackdown, despite waning public support for its policies. Trump had asked allies over the past several days whether they believed Miller would be a suitable choice to replace Wiles, one person familiar with the conversations said. He also raised Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as a possible candidate, the person said.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — whom some in the GOP have sought to blame for the party's losses because of his leadership on the Iran war — welcomed the news, saying in a post on X that Miller "never backs down" and vowing his support.

Some Homeland Security officials expressed disbelief, while others welcomed the change.

"Trump got his MAGA mojo back," a Department of Homeland Security official said.

CNN previously reported that Miller's power became evident in daily 10 a.m. conference calls with DHS officials, where he demanded updates from agencies and exerted pressure on senior officials who delivered less-than-satisfactory results. Officials would often breathe a sigh of relief when Miller directed his ire at other agencies during the calls.

The intense White House pressure has resulted in immigration enforcement casting a wide net on arrests, including targeting those who do not have criminal records.

Last year, Miller directed ICE officials to meet daily quotas of 3,000 immigration arrests — an unprecedented number that the agency struggled to meet. The White House and DHS have repeatedly denied the existence of arrest quotas. Already, Miller was likely to face scrutiny from the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress, and Rep. Robert Garcia, the ranking member on the House Oversight Committee, reaffirmed Friday he would be a top target.

"Stephen Miller should lawyer up," the California Democrat said.

Wiles is latest high-ranking woman to leave

After the president announced the shakeup, Wiles said in a statement on X that serving Trump was "the honor of a lifetime" and that she was "proud to have been a part of what we've accomplished together."

"While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will," she added.

Wiles is the latest high-ranking woman to depart Trump's administration and be replaced by a man. Trump previously parted ways with women serving as attorney general, Labor secretary and Homeland Security secretary, among others.

Before becoming the first-ever woman to serve as White House chief of staff, Wiles was Trump's campaign manager in the 2024 election. She recently announced she had completed treatment for breast cancer.

Trump cycled through four chiefs of staff during his first term. Wiles lasted longer in the post than any of them. She adopted a strategy that did not seek to fundamentally alter the way Trump carried out the job or change his priorities. Instead, she sought to use influential figures within Trump's orbit to shape his governing agenda.

Trump, who frequently used the term "ice maiden" to describe his no-nonsense top aide, had as recently as last month insisted she would remain in the job for the foreseeable future.

"Susie is here and she's gonna be here for a long time," he said on October 16.

This story has been updated with additional developments.

articles.title: Maioridade penal: apenas 8 de 76 países punem como adulto antes dos 18 | G1
articles.standfirst: Análise da Unicef e levantamento do g1 indicam que regimes mais punitivos ocorrem nas leis de Albânia, Andorra, Armênia, Azerbaijão, Haiti, Lituânia, Polônia e Portugal. No Brasil, Congresso Nacional debate reduzir maioridade de 18 para 16 ou 14 anos.
articles.summary: Com o Congresso Nacional brasileiro debatendo a redução da maioridade penal, dados da Unicef mostram que punir jovens como adultos antes dos 18 anos é exceção entre 76 países.
articles.body:
Os países com maioridade penal inferior a 18 anos são minoria em um grupo de 76 países da América Latina, Europa e do G20 , segundo análise feita pelo Fundo das Nações Unidas para a Infância (Unicef) e levantamento realizado pela CRIN (Child Rights International Network, na tradução Rede Internacional pelos Direitos da Criança). O g1 consolidou os dados.

Da lista, 68 estabelecem 18 anos como idade mínima para que alguém seja julgado como adulto, enquanto oito usam idades mais baixas: Albânia, Andorra, Armênia, Azerbaijão, Haiti, Lituânia, Polônia e Portugal.

O Congresso Nacional brasileiro debate a diminuição da maioridade penal brasileira, hoje em 18 anos. As discussões ocorreram na Câmara dos Deputados e no Senado, com propostas paralelas.

Na última semana, o presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), decidiu aguardar a Câmara votar o assunto primeiro .

A oposição quer uma redução geral de 18 para 16 anos e para 14 anos nos casos de crimes hediondos, como assassinato.

Já o presidente Lula (PT) defendeu a redução da maioridade penal para 16 anos nos crimes hediondos. Foi a primeira vez que o petista, então candidato à reeleição, falou sobre o tema de forma contundente, ao responder a uma pergunta da jornalista Renata Lo Prete, durante entrevista à TV Globo no segundo turno da eleição.

No Congresso, o senador Camilo Santana ( PT -CE), líder do governo, apresentou uma proposta para reduzir a idade de 18 anos para 16 anos no caso de crimes hediondos. É essa a proposta que Lula disse apoiar.

Nenhum dos 19 países do G20 analisados pela Unicef tem maioridade penal abaixo dos 18 anos. Na América Latina, o cenário é semelhante: dos 20 países pesquisados, somente o Haiti tem maioridade penal aos 16 anos.

O levantamento da Unicef foi realizado entre agosto e setembro de 2026 e analisou a legislação de países como Estados Unidos, China, Alemanha, Argentina e Japão, além do Brasil.

O G20 funciona como o principal clube econômico do mundo, reunindo 19 dos países mais influentes do planeta, a União Europeia e a União Africana. Juntos, esses membros controlam 85% de toda a riqueza produzida no mundo (PIB) e 75% do comércio global.

Nos Estados Unidos, por exemplo, a variação se dá em alguns estados do país -- pois lá a legislação estadual pode ser diferente da federal. Na Holanda, isso ocorre com quem tem 16 ou 17 anos, quando um juiz considera que o crime é grave o bastante ou que a personalidade do autor permite que ele responda como adulto pelo crime cometido.

Já o estudo do CRIN com os países europeus é de 2019 e foi atualizado pela reportagem do g1 com base nas leis de cada país listado.

São levados em consideração dois conceitos diferentes:

a maioridade penal , que define a idade a partir da qual uma pessoa pode ser julgada como adulta;

e a idade de responsabilização penal , quando adolescentes já podem responder judicialmente por seus atos, mas em um sistema específico para sua faixa etária.

No Brasil, a maioridade penal é de 18 anos, enquanto a responsabilização de adolescentes começa aos 12 anos , idade em que podem cumprir medidas socioeducativas por atos infracionais.

Brasil entre países que responsabilizam adolescentes mais cedo

Segundo o Unicef, todos os 19 países do G20 analisados possuem sistemas de Justiça separados para adultos e adolescentes que cometem infrações. Em sete deles, há exceções que permitem que adolescentes sejam encaminhados ao sistema penal adulto, mas a regra geral é que sejam julgados pela Justiça juvenil.

O Brasil está entre os países que começam a responsabilizar adolescentes mais cedo . No G20, a idade de 12 anos também é adotada por África do Sul, Canadá, Indonésia, México e Turquia. Em países como Alemanha, Argentina, Itália e Japão, a responsabilização começa aos 14 anos.

Na Albânia, a responsabilização ocorre aos 16 anos para contravenções penais, mas pode ser feita aos 14 anos se a pessoa cometer crimes mais graves, como homicídio.

A França tem responsabilização a partir dos 13 anos, mas a pessoa pode responder antes disso se a Justiça considerar que o autor do crime compreendeu o que seria feito e, mesmo assim, o fez.

Na América Latina, o Brasil também está entre os países com menor idade de responsabilização. Além dele, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Equador, Honduras, México e Panamá estabelecem os 12 anos como idade mínima. Na Argentina, Bolívia, Chile, Colômbia, Paraguai, Peru e Venezuela, por exemplo, o limite é de 14 anos.

Para Joaquin Gonzalez-Aleman, representante do Unicef no Brasil, a redução da maioridade penal pode trazer impactos negativos para o Brasil.

"Hoje, adolescentes que cometem atos infracionais são responsabilizados por meio do Sistema Socioeducativo, em unidades separadas de adultos, com medidas que combinam responsabilização com educação e reintegração social. Levá-los para o sistema prisional adulto pode expô-los a redes criminosas mais estruturadas e aumentar o risco de recrutamento pelo crime organizado", diz.

Segundo o especialista, dados do Conselho Nacional de Justiça (CNJ) mostram que "a reentrada no sistema prisional entre adultos é quase o dobro da observada entre adolescentes no Sistema Socioeducativo, o que reforça a importância de investir em respostas capazes de reduzir a reincidência".

"Aqui passamos a falar não apenas de impactos para os adolescentes, mas para a sociedade como um todo: se os adolescentes passarem para o sistema adulto, com a redução da maioridade penal, é provável que as taxas de reincidências deles também aumentem e que a sociedade sofra com mais crimes", diz.

Segundo Gonzalez-Aleman, a redução também pode impactar o Brasil no cenário internacional.

"A regra atual, de maioridade penal aos 18 anos, está alinhada ao padrão predominante internacionalmente: nenhum dos 19 países do G20 analisados pelo Unicef estabelece, como regra geral, uma idade inferior a 18 anos. Uma redução afastaria o Brasil desse padrão e das evidências internacionais sobre uma justiça juvenil adequada à idade e ao desenvolvimento dos adolescentes."

O levantamento também aponta mudanças recentes na legislação de outros países. Na Argentina , uma alteração aprovada em fevereiro de 2026 reduziu de 16 para 14 anos a idade de responsabilização penal . A maioridade penal, no entanto, permaneceu em 18 anos.

Nos Estados Unidos, estados como Nova York, Connecticut e Carolina do Norte fizeram o caminho inverso: mudaram suas legislações para que adolescentes de 16 e 17 anos, que antes podiam ser julgados como adultos, passassem a responder à Justiça juvenil: "Viram que [as medidas] não produziram os resultados esperados", diz o representante do Unicef.

Segundo o Unicef, as mudanças como nos estados americanos ocorreram após avaliações de que tratar adolescentes como adultos perante a Justiça não contribuiu para reduzir a criminalidade ou para melhorar a segurança pública.

“Os países mais ricos do mundo, onde vivem cerca de 60% da população mundial, concordam que é possível responsabilizar um adolescente sem tratá-lo como adulto”, afirmou Joaquin Gonzalez-Aleman.

Para o representante, a separação entre os sistemas de Justiça adulto e juvenil permite que adolescentes tenham acesso à educação, saúde e assistência social, com o objetivo de favorecer a reintegração deles à sociedade e evitar a reincidência.

O Unicef também alerta que colocar adolescentes e adultos no mesmo sistema prisional pode produzir o efeito contrário ao esperado, aproximando jovens de organizações criminosas e rompendo vínculos com a escola, a família e a comunidade.

“Responsabilizar adolescentes que cometem atos infracionais é necessário. Mas, para isso, não é preciso tratá-lo como adulto”, disse Gonzalez-Aleman.

No Brasil, adolescentes entre 12 e 17 anos que cometem atos infracionais podem ser submetidos a medidas socioeducativas, previstas no Estatuto da Criança e do Adolescente (ECA). Entre elas estão advertência, obrigação de reparar o dano, prestação de serviços à comunidade, liberdade assistida, semiliberdade e internação.

Assim, ter uma idade de responsabilização menor não significa necessariamente ter uma maioridade penal menor. É essa distinção que, segundo o Unicef, explica por que o Brasil responsabiliza adolescentes a partir dos 12 anos, mas mantém a maioridade penal aos 18.

Segundo Joaquin Gonzalez-Aleman, do Unicef, a idade mínima de responsabilidade penal no Brasil está abaixo da recomendação mais atual do Comitê dos Direitos da Criança, que é de 14 anos.

"Essa diretriz, atualizada em 2019, justifica-se pela etapa diferenciada de desenvolvimento físico e psicológico de crianças e adolescentes, e é observada por quase 40% dos países do G20 e América Latina. É um debate legítimo para o país, mas é importante não confundi-lo com a maioridade penal: uma coisa é definir a partir de quando um adolescente pode ser responsabilizado; outra é definir quando deve passar a ser tratado como adulto pelo sistema penal", explica.

articles.title: Estiagem em Manaus transforma paisagem e afeta 129 mil pessoas | G1
articles.standfirst: Entre junho e novembro de 2026, a paisagem marcada pela cheia dos rios deu lugar a áreas de solo exposto, bancos de areia, acúmulo de lixo e fumaça no horizonte.
articles.summary: A estiagem em Manaus expõe solo, lixo e gera crise no abastecimento, levando o Amazonas a decretar emergência em saúde após afetar milhares de moradores.
articles.body:
O cenário de diferentes pontos de Manaus mudou radicalmente em um intervalo de cinco meses. Entre junho e novembro de 2026, a paisagem marcada pela cheia dos rios deu lugar a áreas de solo exposto, bancos de areia, acúmulo de lixo e fumaça no horizonte . Os registros feitos pelo g1 mostram a transformação de pontos estratégicos da capital durante a transição entre os períodos de cheia e vazante.

Um dos locais que apontam para essa mudança é a Marina do Davi, na Zona Oeste de Manaus. No local de embarque e desembarque de pessoas que chegam ou acessam as comunidades ribeirinhas, a equipe do g1 encontrou estruturas flutuantes apoiadas sobre o solo, em meio às dificuldades de deslocamento enfrentadas por moradores e trabalhadores que dependem do transporte fluvial.

A mudança também pode ser observada na área portuária da cidade, a partir do Mirante Lúcia Almeida, na região central da capital. Nas imagens registradas em junho, a água ocupava grande parte da paisagem. Agora, com a descida do nível do Rio Negro, áreas estão expostas, revelando um cenário completamente diferente. Também houve registros de lixos às margens do rio.

O g1 percorreu, ainda, a Orla do São Raimundo e a Praia da Ponta Negra, nas zonas Sul e Oeste, respectivamente. A mudança da paisagem também é evidente: no São Raimundo, um flutuante, que durante a cheia estava no rio, ficou encalhado na área da região portuária, e onde antes estava coberto por rio, agora tem veículos de transporte de cargas.

Maíra Oliveira é moradora da região da Marina do Davi, no bairro Tarumã, na Zona Oeste da cidade. Ela relatou que a vazante dificulta a rotina de quem vive e trabalha nas comunidades próximas.

“Tem sido bastante difícil por causa da vazante. Os flutuantes ficam todos na terra e isso dificulta muito a locomoção. Também tem a questão de quem sai para trabalhar", disse.

A queda no nível da água também afeta o abastecimento. De acordo com Maíra, moradores que utilizam poços enfrentam o risco de ficar sem água quando a seca se intensifica.

“Quem fica em flutuante usa poço. Se secar muito, o poço também seca e a gente acaba ficando sem água”, explicou.

Outro problema apontado é o acúmulo de lixo nas margens e nos igarapés. Segundo a moradora, resíduos são carregados pela enxurrada durante as chuvas e acabam se acumulando na região. Apesar disso, ela avalia que o volume de lixo deixado pela vazante deste ano foi menor que o registrado no ano passado.

“Quando chove, vem bastante lixo. Mas, nesta seca, não veio tanto quanto no ano passado. A gente também faz um trabalho comunitário de limpeza, junto com a presidente daqui, recolhendo os resíduos ao redor”, afirmou.

Seca do Rio Negro expõe lixo nas proximidades da Marina do Davi, em Manaus. — Foto: José Lima/Rede Amazônica

Maíra também cobrou mais atenção do poder público para melhorar a infraestrutura da região. Ela destacou a necessidade de novas pontes para facilitar o acesso às comunidades, especialmente para pessoas com mobilidade reduzida, além de melhorias no abastecimento de água.

“Eu queria que o poder público olhasse mais para a gente. Conseguimos um poço depois de muita luta, porque dependemos de água para beber. Aqui já existe uma ponte, mas precisamos de outra que faça a ligação com a comunidade, porque é muito difícil chegar até aqui”, pediu.

Segundo boletim mais recente, divulgado pelo Governo do Amazonas na terça-feira (3), mais de 129,7 mil pessoas já foram afetadas pela estiagem no estado . Os dados são da Defesa Civil estadual, responsável por coordenar as ações de enfrentamento aos impactos da seca.

O levantamento aponta que 47 municípios estão em situação de emergência : Alvarães, Amaturá, Anamã, Anori, Apuí, Atalaia do Norte, Autazes, Barreirinha, Benjamin Constant, Boca do Acre, Borba, Boa Vista do Ramos, Caapiranga, Carauari, Careiro, Careiro da Várzea e Coari.

Também integram a lista Eirunepé, Envira, Humaitá, Ipixuna, Itamarati, Japurá, Juruá, Jutaí, Lábrea, Manacapuru, Manaquiri, Manicoré, Maraã, Maués, Nhamundá, Nova Olinda do Norte, Novo Airão, Novo Aripuanã, Parintins, Pauini, Presidente Figueiredo, Rio Preto da Eva, Santo Antônio do Içá, São Paulo de Olivença, Silves, Tapauá, Tefé, Tonantins, Uarini e Urucurituba.

Até 27 de outubro, o Governo do Amazonas realizou ações de assistência em 15 municípios. Foram distribuídas 4,8 mil cestas básicas, o equivalente a aproximadamente 96 toneladas de alimentos, além de 3,4 mil kits de limpeza, 3.060 caixas d’água com capacidade para 500 litros, três reservatórios de 5 mil litros e 18 kits purificadores de água.

Um dia antes, em 26 de outubro, o Executivo estadual decretou situação de emergência em saúde pública por 180 dias devido aos impactos da estiagem severa no estado. A medida foi publicada no Diário Oficial e levou em consideração o isolamento de comunidades, as dificuldades de transporte de materiais de saúde e os problemas no atendimento à população.

Segundo o decreto, um levantamento preliminar da Defesa Civil estadual identificou 562 comunidades isoladas pela seca dos rios. A situação dificulta o acesso dos moradores aos serviços de saúde e pode comprometer o transporte de pacientes e o abastecimento de medicamentos e oxigênio medicinal.

articles.title: How Scott Colom turned his Mississippi Senate race into a nail-biter
articles.summary: Mississippi Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) is fighting for her political life as Democrat Scott Colom threatens to pull off one of the biggest upsets of the midte...
articles.body:
Mississippi Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) is fighting for her political life as Democrat Scott Colom threatens to pull off one of the biggest upsets of the midterms in a state that hasn't elected a Democratic senator since 1982.

Before polls closed Tuesday, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) gave Hyde-Smith a 91 percent chance of winning her race. But by late Friday afternoon, Colom led by 2,734 votes in DDHQ's tally, with thousands of ballots still outstanding.

Some of Colom's biggest gains have come in counties Hyde-Smith won handily six years ago. In the Memphis suburbs, he leads by roughly 6 points in DeSoto County, which she carried by 16 points in 2020. On the Gulf Coast, the incumbent's lead in Harrison County has narrowed from 17 points in 2020 to about 4 points in the latest unofficial count.

Colom has also picked up votes in places where Republicans still led by wide margins. In Pearl River County, Colom drew about 4,000 votes, or 24 percent, in the preliminary count — compared with the 2,400 votes, or 22 percent, that Democratic gubernatorial nominee Brandon Presley got in 2023. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won 16 percent of the vote in 2024.

Colom benefited from a national political environment that favored Democrats, but he also gave voters in Mississippi a local target for their frustration over rising prices by turning Hyde-Smith's suggestion that shoppers choose a cheaper protein into a pitch to "pick another senator."

Organizers worked to turn out Black voters, and preliminary returns show about 10 percent more votes were cast in majority-Black counties than in the 2023 governor's race. The New York Times estimated that 91 percent of Black voters back Colom.

The Times's preliminary estimates show a shift toward Democrats across age, race, gender and education groups compared with 2024. Hyde-Smith still led among white voters by 49 points, but that was 19 points narrower than President Trump's margin with those voters two years earlier.

New Southern Majority, a super PAC launched by the Southern Poverty Law Center's political advocacy arm, saw an opening to reach GOP voters while other organizations focused on turning out Black voters this cycle, according to Brannon Miller, whose consulting firm, Chism Strategies, ran the effort.

He said the group spent just under $1 million on messaging to Republican voters in the race, targeting about 200,000 Republicans with messages that focused almost entirely on criticizing Hyde-Smith over issues including the war in Iran, high gas prices, tariffs and her support for data centers.

Miller suggested that messaging was effective, pointing to Colom's gains in red counties like Pearl River and DeSoto as a sign that some voters who typically back Republicans crossed over this cycle.

"There's literally no other explanation," Miller said. "These are places where Democrats get less than 15 percent of the vote in a presidential year. There are not Democrats there to turn out."

"So when Scott Colom doubles the number of votes that Brandon Presley got in some of these counties, or close to it, that has to be coming from white Republicans flipping and voting for the first Black senator since Reconstruction," he continued.

DeSoto stands out as the county that saw the biggest swing toward Democrats from the 2024 presidential race. Trump carried the fast-growing Memphis suburbs by 24 points in 2024, but Colom is now leading by roughly 6 points, accounting for a 30-point shift over just two years. Colom drew about 28,100 votes in the county, nearly twice as many as Presley received there in 2023.

"In my mind, a big part of the swing is explained by the opposition to data centers," Miller said, pointing to a facility in DeSoto that has drawn significant backlash from locals about persistent noise issues.

DeSoto County Democratic Party Chair Deborah Williams said she also thought the backlash to the data center might have hurt Hyde-Smith's support, but she attributed more of the swing to the work organizers did, knocking on nearly 70,000 doors and working to increase absentee ballots.

She also said she thinks voters weren't excited about Hyde-Smith and that Colom's "Mississippi Matters" message resonated especially with young voters. On Election Day, she said she went from precinct to precinct and was surprised to see just how many young voters were lining up at the polls. She said some were waiting two or three hours in the rain just to get a chance to vote.

"[Mississippi] had been perceived as a deep-red state, but it really wasn't a deep-red state. It was a state where people weren't engaged in this process for a number of different reasons," Williams said. "So yes, I think Scott had a lot to do with bringing that sense of pride back to the state of Mississippi, and people did embrace that."

Arekia Bennett-Scott, executive director of Mississippi Votes, said young people have been organizing in the state for years but the push to redraw Mississippi's congressional districts gave them a particular reason to show up this year.

Bennett-Scott noted that many students saw redistricting as a threat to Black political representation and responded by rallying in Jackson in May and organizing across campuses.

"They understand that voting is a tool, not the only tool, but it's a tool that they can fight back with this particular election cycle," she said, referring to youth turnout.

The Times estimated that voters under 30 in Mississippi backed Colom, 62 percent to 33 percent — a whopping 44-point swing toward Democrats compared with 2024.

But the political organizer emphasized that the higher youth engagement is not about any single candidate or party.

"Young people are fighting towards power, and that speaks to the way that they showed up," Bennett-Scott said, adding, "They know what's at stake, and they align themselves with what and who was speaking the language of justice for them in this moment."

The razor-thin margins in the deep-red Mississippi Senate race took many political observers by surprise, but local organizers note that the state has gotten a lot more competitive in recent years and people are only now paying attention.

"I think that there's a stereotype of the state as being what it was in the 1960s that just no longer holds," Miller said.

"It's not like this is a new Mississippi," he continued. "This is the Mississippi that's been there for at least the past decade. This was just finally when all of the right confluence of circumstances came together to allow us to win."

articles.title: Latino vote helped thwart Texas Republicans' redistricting effort
articles.summary: The GOP lost all four redrawn districts in the heavily Latino Rio Grande Valley.
articles.body:
Last year, the Republican-controlled Texas legislature redrew its congressional maps in a controversial mid-decade redistricting effort aimed at giving the GOP five more House seats. Encouraged by President Donald Trump's strong showing among Hispanic voters in 2024, they concentrated on four districts in the heavily Latino Rio Grande Valley in South Texas.

But the Latino vote in Texas swung back from the president on Tuesday, driven by its dissatisfaction with Trump's immigration policy and the economy, according to ABC News' Voter Poll. Republicans failed to flip any of the Rio Grand Valley districts -- losing by double-digits in all of them -- and ended up with a net loss of one House seat.

Hispanic voters comprise more than 30% of eligible Texas voters and are especially concentrated in four counties in the Rio Grande Valley, where they make up more than 90% of the population, according to U.S. census data.

ABC News' Voter Poll showed 67% of Hispanics who voted in the state's Senate race said the Trump administration's actions on immigration enforcement have gone too far, compared to 45% of white Senate voters.

Jon Taylor, a University of Texas at San Antonio political science professor, told ABC affiliate KSAT that this issue is especially influential in the Rio Grande Valley saying, "A number of people living in South Texas, living in San Antonio, who had family, friends, somebody they knew who got picked up in an ICE raid. It had a profound impact on voting."

About 83% of Hispanic voters said the economy was not so good or poor, compared to 63% of white voters, according to ABC News' Voter Poll, and 75% of Hispanics who voted in the Senate race said that Trump's economic policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S., compared to 52% of white voters.

The Rio Grande Valley has some of the highest rates of poverty in the country. Héctor E. Sánchez Barba, who leads Mi Familia Vota, a leading Latino political group, told ABC News that the Valley has been particularly hurt by the Trump's economic policies, saying "It's very clear the economic impact that these policies are having is on mostly working-class, people-of-color communities."

All four of the Rio Grande Valley counties saw voter turnout up from 2022: Up 9.9% in Hidalgo County; 7.9% higher in Cameron County; a 7.4% increase in Willacy County; and 3.3% higher in Starr County. The state saw an overall increase of about 6% in voter turnout from 2022.

Additionally, Democrats flipped two largely Hispanic districts in South Texas that Trump had previously won by double digit margins.

And the blue wave extended to Democrats winning all statewide races.

ABC News Voter polls showed that Hispanic voters backed Democratic Senate Candidate James Talarico with 68% of the vote and Democratic governor candidate Gina Hinojosa with 65%.

Barba said they won because "Their policies are a reflection of working class families" and a "reflection of inclusion."

Barba said the Democratic victories could make the state a presidential battleground in 2028.

"Make no mistake, anybody that wants to become a president in 2028 has to come through the Latino community."

articles.title: Justice Department drops bid to force California to set aside ballots from alleged noncitizens
articles.summary: The Trump administration’s efforts to separate out thousands of ballots were thwarted in the federal judiciary, all the way up to the Supreme Court.
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — The U.S. Department of Justice on Friday moved to dismiss its own lawsuit that sought to stop California from counting roughly 20,000 ballots it alleged went to noncitizens until their immigration status could be verified. The request to dismiss the case comes days after Republicans' significant losses in the midterm elections and about a week before a scheduled hearing where a special master was slated to evaluate the accuracy of the list. California officials have previously said the list is out of date and includes legitimate voters — a sentiment that the federal judge presiding over the case echoed in his blistering order denying the federal government's request. The case was at the forefront of President Donald Trump's administration's effort to assert control over state-run elections across the country, which Trump has said are rife with illegal voting without providing evidence. The Department of Justice remains enmeshed in litigation with immigrant and voting rights groups seeking to limit its use of the list of what is says are suspected noncitizens. Another controversial suit it filed in Alaska at Trump’s direction before the election to block the victory of the Democrat in that state’s Senate race was swiftly dismissed by a federal judge. The administration is appealing that ruling but has yet to file a full brief at the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals. California had processed roughly 9 million ballots as of early Friday, with nearly 5 million still left to be counted, according to state election officials. The motion to dismiss the lawsuit said that, by the time of the upcoming hearing, the state will have already irreparably "commingled the challenged ballots with lawful ones." “The relief the United States sought and needed is no longer available—rendering voluntary dismissal necessary,” the motion said. Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, previously argued in court that the lawsuit would be irrelevant after Election Day, because there would be no way to sequester the ones allegedly belonging to noncitizens. The lawsuit was filed in mid-October, when ballots had been sent to all of the state's 23 million registered voters, and after hundreds of thousands of ballots were already processed. Once a ballot is processed, it is completely anonymized. Essayli said at the time the lawsuit was filed that his goal was to “safeguard the integrity of the election so it doesn't have an effect on the upcoming election." “We want to stop the illegal voting. We don't want to chase it later,” he said outside of court the week before the election. The United States Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California referred all questions to the Department of Justice in Washington, D.C., which did not respond to an emailed request for comment on Friday evening. California prosecutors in recent weeks have arrested over 30 noncitizens who are accused of illegally registering to vote. Some who were arrested were also accused of voting in previous elections. Elections clerks around California in the week before the election were sent subpoenas to testify before grand juries slated to convene in November. It's not clear who is being criminally charged in those cases, but the department does not typically subpoena people whom it regards as targets of a criminal investigation to appear before a grand jury. U.S. District Judge David O. Carter appointed the special master in late October, shortly after allowing California to proceed with elections as planned. Carter, who was appointed by former President Bill Clinton, argued in his blistering order that separating ballots at that late stage would risk disenfranchising citizens and warned it would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections. The special master would have also considered whether or not California election officials did in fact have a mechanism for separating the ballots.

articles.title: Trump Signals More Cabinet Changes in Store After GOP Losses
articles.summary: Trump Signals More Cabinet Changes in Store After GOP Losses
articles.body:
President Donald Trump said Friday he expects to make additional Cabinet changes following Republicans' sweeping midterm election defeats, signaling that the replacement of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles may be only the beginning of a broader administration shake-up.

In an interview with CBS News' "60 Minutes," Trump acknowledged that more personnel changes could be coming but declined to identify which officials might be affected.

Asked whether he expected to fire anyone after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress, Trump replied, "I do, yeah. Little bit."

"I love my Cabinet. I think they're good," Trump said. "But I'll ... be doing maybe a few changes."

The remarks came as Trump announced Friday that longtime senior adviser Stephen Miller would replace Wiles as White House chief of staff, effective Monday.

Trump's comments were made during an interview with CBS News correspondent Ross Douthat scheduled to air Sunday, with excerpts released Friday.

The president's remarks also come amid growing speculation about the future of War Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose handling of the war in Iran has drawn criticism following the GOP's midterm losses.

CBS News reported Wednesday that Trump had privately asked advisers whether Hegseth should remain in his position, citing multiple sources familiar with the discussions.

The network reported that Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis had been floated as a possible replacement, although other sources said Trump had made no decision to remove Hegseth.

Trump publicly expressed confidence in Hegseth when questioned Wednesday and again during the CBS interview.

"I do," Trump replied Friday when asked whether he retained confidence in Hegseth.

"Look, we've won two wars," the president added, referring to U.S. military operations in Venezuela and Iran.

Hegseth also faces the prospect of intensified congressional scrutiny when Democrats take control of the House and Senate in January.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Friday that Hegseth should leave office but stopped short of endorsing impeachment proceedings, according to NPR.

"He's got to go," Jeffries said during an interview with NPR's "Morning Edition."

Asked whether Democrats should pursue impeachment, Jeffries replied, "I don't want to get out ahead of the caucus."

NPR also reported that Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., has threatened to force a House vote on eight articles of impeachment unless Hegseth resigns.

Meanwhile, Trump's decision to elevate Miller places one of his closest advisers in charge of White House operations as Democrats prepare to challenge administration policies and launch congressional investigations.

CBS News reported Friday that Miller, previously deputy chief of staff, has played a central role in shaping Trump's immigration enforcement and deportation policies.

His appointment could also set the stage for a more confrontational relationship with incoming Democrat congressional leaders, who have sharply criticized the administration's immigration agenda.

Trump, however, rejected suggestions that Wiles' departure was prompted by the election results.

"It's just time. Sometimes you change," Trump told reporters Friday, according to CNN.

CBS News separately reported that Wiles submitted her resignation Thursday and that her departure was tied to the Republican election defeats, citing three sources familiar with the matter.

Trump praised Miller as a trusted and effective adviser.

"He's been with me right from the beginning ... he's very loyal, smart. Does a great job," Trump said, according to CNN.

"He's been an MVP every year. He's been just great. So, we're very happy with him," the president added.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, has specifically identified Miller as a target for investigation.

"Oversight Democrats will continue to investigate Miller for his misconduct," Garcia said in a statement Friday reported by Mediaite.

"Stephen Miller should lawyer up," Garcia added.

CBS News also reported that Garcia had singled out Miller and other administration officials as potential investigative targets following Tuesday's elections.

The White House has dismissed the prospect of such inquiries as politically motivated.

"If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told CBS News.

articles.title: DOJ dismisses lawsuit over California’s 20,000 disputed ballots
articles.summary: The Justice Department (DOJ) requested Friday to dismiss its lawsuit against California, which sought to make the state’s election officials set aside roughly 20,000 ballots for voters the federal government alleged were not U.S. citizens. The Supreme Court already ruled against the Trump administration in an emergency order ahead of Election Day, preventing them from…
articles.body:
The Justice Department (DOJ) requested Friday to dismiss its lawsuit against California, which sought to make the state’s election officials set aside roughly 20,000 ballots for voters the federal government alleged were not U.S. citizens.

The Supreme Court already ruled against the Trump administration in an emergency order ahead of Election Day, preventing them from forcing California to set aside the ballots. A federal judge had previously blocked the administration’s request.

The DOJ had sought to prevent the state from counting the ballots until the voters’ immigration status could be verified.

The motion comes after Republicans faced sweeping losses in Tuesday’s midterms, during which they lost at least seven Senate and 42 House seats — and more races still outstanding.

The DOJ’s California lawsuit was one of several the agency brought forth ahead of Election Day. The Trump administration had also filed a lawsuit in Alaska seeking to block the state’s election certification if incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) lost, arguing the presence of another candidate on the ballot, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., could have confused voters.

A judge dismissed that lawsuit before Election Day, but the Trump administration vowed to appeal. As of Friday, Sullivan narrowly trails his Democratic opponent, Mary Peltola, in the Senate race — but no winner has been projected, as thousands of votes remain uncounted.

Accusations of noncitizen voting are not new for the Trump administration, which has sent threatening letters to state election officials and demanded states turn over their voter rolls to identify non-U.S. citizens.

Earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) accused Nevada of having nearly 16,000 possible noncitizens on its voter rolls. DHS later revised that number down to 185, but when Nevada officials investigated, they found all of those identified were actually U.S. citizens, The New York Times reported.

Noncitizen voting is permitted in some local elections but is illegal federally. Multiple studies have found that noncitizen voting is not widespread in U.S. elections.

On Election Day, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin threatened any noncitizens who tried to vote with a warning.

“If you vote illegally in this country, and you are NOT eligible to vote, [DHS] will find you, hunt you down, and you will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law,” Mullin wrote on social platform X.

articles.title: 'Defeated Goliath': Did faith help Democrats flip key midterm races?
articles.summary: Religion proved pivotal in the 2026 midterms as voters shifted toward Democrats in key races nationwide.
articles.body:
As Democrat James Talarico of Texas delivered his acceptance speech Tuesday in Austin after his decisive U.S. Senate race win over Republican Ken Paxton , a large placard in front of him featured the words, "Love Thy Neighbor."

That message seemed to resonate with voters nationwide, who vastly backed Democrats in a sweeping series of victories that some saw as a humanitarian rejection of federal policies such as overly aggressive immigration enforcement, unauthorized war, efforts to stamp out diversity and economic measures that have left many families struggling.

Religion proved pivotal at the ballot box nationwide, experts say, shaping voter views on key issues that turned previously red states blue. Faith was also brandished by candidates like Talarico to appeal to the electorate, even as conservatives blasted his progressive Christianity; in some cases, religion was weaponized by opponents, as in Islamophobic attacks and ad campaigns in Michigan and Texas.

Who is James Talarico? Meet the new Texas Senator

"You did see some rejection of Republicans, especially with Hispanic Catholics in Texas," said Michael Moreland, director of the Eleanor H. McCullen Center for Law, Religion and Public Policy at Villanova University in Pennsylvania. "Especially along the South Texas border, aspects of the administration's immigration enforcement alienated a lot of voters. President Trump in 2024 peeled off a lot of those voters, but he lost them Tuesday night."

Democrat megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton flipped a U.S. Senate seat in Kansas, while in Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton was elected both the state's first Jewish and female governor, her Judaism informing her progressive platform.

Meanwhile, a record seven Muslims were elected to Congress nationwide, including Democrat physician Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who became the nation's first Muslim U.S. senator. The number could rise to eight, depending on how California Democrat Aisha Wahab fares in her race for the state's 14 th Congressional district seat.

Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian and grandson of a Baptist preacher, was among several candidates who charted rare territory for white Democrats by making religion a central part of his campaign, citing scripture and stressing his Biblical grounding.

Dubbed " Talafreako " by President Donald Trump , Talarico kicked off his acceptance speech by using the Bible story of David and Goliath as a metaphor for his race against Paxton and "billionaire megadonors" like Elon Musk , who spent nearly $230 million to support Paxton's campaign against Talarico.

"We went up against our own Goliath – the richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world and the entire D.C. establishment," Talarico said. Comparing himself to the shepherd boy who wielded a slingshot to slay his mightier foe, he told the crowd: "You were my slingshot. The people of Texas were my slingshot. And tonight, we defeated Goliath."

Swing to Dems more pronounced among some faiths

Nationwide, exit polls conducted by NBC News revealed sizable shifts among several groups in the midterms compared to the 2024 election . Just under half of Catholics backed Republican candidates in the midterms , NBC found, compared to 59% who voted for Trump in 2024.

Jewish voters, meanwhile, swung the other way, NBC found: While 78% supported Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris in 2024, 68% voted for Democrats in this year's midterms.

"Donald Trump said voters should pretend he was on the ballot in the midterms, and Jewish Americans did just that," Halie Soifer, CEO of the Jewish Democratic Council of America, said in a statement. "Jewish voters are not a monolith, but they widely disapprove of Donald Trump. This, coupled with the strength of the Democratic candidates who flipped red seats blue, led to overwhelming support for Democrats among Jewish voters in this election."

Among religiously unaffiliated voters, NBC found, 27% supported Trump in 2024, compared to 20% who favored Republican candidates this fall.

Meanwhile, 86% of Muslims supported Democratic candidates in 2026 – the share wasn't tallied in 2024 – while slightly fewer Protestants or other Christians supported Republican candidates this year compared with 2024.

Exit polls conducted by the Council on American-Islamic Relations indicated the Iran war, the economy, rising Islamophobia and Israel's war in Gaza were foremost in their midterm voting choices. "Rising Islamophobia strengthened their motivation to vote," the council said in a statement . "They overwhelmingly backed Democrats, but many remain unconvinced that either party listens to their concerns."

During his race for Michigan's Senate seat, El-Sayed was dismissed as a " jihadist " by Trump and accused of links to terrorist groups, both without evidence. Others criticized him for what they saw as a failure to sufficiently denounce antisemitism.

Frank Lacopo, an assistant professor of history at Southeast Missouri State University in Cape Girardeau, said such comments backfired with voters concerned with other issues.

"It really seems like El-Sayed's more secular messaging on affordability was more effective," Lacopo said. "What he showed people in Michigan was a vision of an American who happens to be Muslim."

Did Catholics feel betrayed by Trump, GOP?

More than 50 million Catholics live in the U.S., with about 53% identifying as Republican, according to the Pew Research Center . Accounting for about a quarter of U.S. voters, they represent a broad political spectrum.

"It's hard to neatly categorize the Catholic vote, because it depends on other factors – whether they're white Catholics, Hispanic Catholics, young Catholics or more churchgoing ones," Moreland said.

Kelsey Reinhardt, president and CEO of Catholic Vote, a conservative political advocacy organization based in Carmel, Indiana, said Catholics' midterm swing toward Democrats reflected the broad concerns of the American electorate.

"In this election, Catholics are representative of the American population writ large," Reinhardt said. "They care about necessities. The socioeconomic stratosphere of Catholics is pretty ordinary."

In 2024, she said, Catholic voters largely believed Trump would be a greater arbiter of Catholic values. This time around, some may have felt betrayed by Trump's broken anti-war promises, while anti-abortion advocates likely felt the president hasn't done enough to advance their cause.

"The Catholic vote is soft Republican when there's a Republican who advances their ideals," Reinhardt said. "But they swing back when they feel their values are not being met. The Iran war was a factor too, but I'm not sure whether it's an issue because it was declared immoral by the pope or because people didn't want a forever war."

Catholic concerns loomed large at the state level, such as in Virginia , where local bishops led a furious campaign that unsuccessfully sought to mobilize voters to reject ballot measures expanding abortion rights and removing wordage in the state constitution strictly defining marriage as between a man and woman.

"That was one where Catholics were heroic in their efforts," Reinhardt said. "But 700,000 Catholics in Virginia won't overturn the majority there."

Lacopo thinks a factor that may have been a factor in Catholics' Democratic swing is the Catholic church's growing presence online.

"It's important not to underestimate the power that Catholic church messaging on social media has on Catholics," he said. "Even if they're not practicing Catholics. A lot of Americans began to subscribe to Vatican News when Leo became pope, and they identify with him as an American."

Pope Leo XIV's fluency in both English and Spanish allows him to reach a wide swath of voters, he said. Meanwhile, the pope's social media features a constant feed of direct quotes from the Chicago-born pontiff that help American followers see him as someone representing "a more accepting, open-arms version of Christianity."

In general, Lacopo feels Democrats fielded better quality candidates who appealed to voters, with faith part of the package in states like Texas and Kansas.

"Talarico was absolutely perfect as a candidate for Texas because he had a way of speaking that came from his background of training as a Presbyterian minister," Lacopo said. "He was able to use Christian messaging in a way that couldn't be countered by Republicans."

He noted Talarico's acceptance speech also focused on what many consider the central tenets of Christian teaching, the notion of loving God and one's neighbor – a message he thinks resonated not just with Texas Latinos anxious over immigration policy but with the kind of voters who plant signs reading "No Human Being is Illegal" in their front yards.

"I'm surprised and not surprised at the same time that Democrats have taken so long to latch on to that," Lacopo said. "Even if you're a secular voter and don't practice religion, you can relate to the second part of that message."

articles.title: Former GOP governor: ‘Wisconsin is a blue state’
articles.summary: Former Wisconsin Gov. Tommy Thompson (R) declared the Badger State blue in a post-election interview Wednesday, pointing to recent statewide defeats for the GOP — including in its gubernatorial race. “Wisconsin is no longer a purple state,” Thompson told Wisconsin Public Radio. “We haven’t won a statewide race for a long time. Wisconsin is a…
articles.body:
Former Wisconsin Gov. Tommy Thompson (R) declared the Badger State blue in a post-election interview Wednesday, pointing to recent statewide defeats for the GOP — including in its gubernatorial race.

“Wisconsin is no longer a purple state,” Thompson told Wisconsin Public Radio. “We haven’t won a statewide race for a long time. Wisconsin is a blue state, and it was before I got elected governor. And it’s gone back to that.”

Thompson was first elected in 1986 and served for four terms — making him the longest-serving governor in the state’s history. While the former governor won his race by wide margins, this year’s GOP candidate, Rep. Tom Tiffany, lost the race to Democrat David Crowley by 8 points on election night.

Republicans have won statewide races in Wisconsin in recent years — notably President Trump’s wins in 2016 and 2018 as well as Sen. Ron Johnson’s 2016 and 2022 victories. Thompson wrote the GOP’s recent success off as an anomaly, pointing to races for state supreme court that conservative-aligned candidates lost by wide margins.

“Trump was an aberration, but Wisconsin is still a blue state,” Thompson said. “You guys have got to realize that. And nobody can convince me this is a purple state anymore when you lose the supreme court justices by 15, 20 percent … and you lose the governorship by 8 points.”2

A conservative-aligned justice has not won election to the Wisconsin Supreme Court since 2019, and liberal-aligned candidates have claimed clear victories in 2020, 2023, 2025 and, most recently, a 20-point victory in 2026. In some cases, the races have received outsized attention, such as when Elon Musk poured $25 million into the contest in 2025 to support conservative candidates, but liberal-leaning Susan Crawford ended up winning by 10 points.

Though Wisconsin’s presidential races have remained close. Excluding former President Obama’s two races, where he carried the state easily, no presidential candidate has received a majority of the vote while winning Wisconsin since Michael Dukakis in 1988. In the last three presidential elections, the winning candidate claimed victory by less than one point.

Going forward, Thompson said the GOP needs to “rebuild,” arguing state Republicans have ignored Dane County — which includes the state’s capital, Madison — and Milwaukee County, two of the most populous and bluest counties in the state.

“I probably am the only Republican that’s ever carried Dane County when I was governor, and I carried Milwaukee County twice. And that’s because I spent a heck of a lot of time there,” Thompson said.

“If you want to overlook these counties you’re never gonna win,” he added. “Simple as that.”

articles.title: With death sentence clemency, Newsom takes another big political risk
articles.summary: Amid speculation about how the mass commutation could help or hurt his presidential prospects in 2028, Gov. Gavin Newsom's decision pushes the boundaries of...
articles.body:
While running for California governor in 2018, Gavin Newsom declared that he would rather be bold and fail than retreat to the safety of mediocrity.

The two-term governor known for taking big political risks once again made good on that vow Thursday when he moved to offer clemency to every inmate sentenced to death in California.

Amid a hum of speculation about how the mass commutation could help or hurt his presidential prospects in 2028, the Democratic politician sent a clear, defining message to Americans about where he stands and the type of leader they could expect.

"If my job is just to read the polls, you can have an AI chatbot as governor," Newsom said in an interview Friday. "I was hired for my judgment, and like it or hate it, that was why I think I was given this privilege, and that's the responsibility of a leader. My job's leadership, not stewardship. It's not management. It's to lead.

"I'm here to change polls, change minds."

The sweeping decision comes more than 20 years after Newsom emerged in the national consciousness when, as mayor of San Francisco, he defied federal law and allowed same-sex marriages in the City by the Bay.

Bold moves that test the limits of his power, such as a controversial, first-in-the-nation stay-at-home order during the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic and spearheading Proposition 50 last year to redraw California's congressional districts to offset Republican attempts to gerrymander red states, have defined his leadership, for good or bad.

The Democratic governor said those kinds of decisions are "sort of embedded in my DNA." About a decade ago he said he was pushed to describe his core motivation. Though he admits it sounds trite, the governor said: "It's to stand up for ideals and strike out against injustice."

The death penalty, he said, is not handed out equally. He quoted Bryan Stevenson, the founder of Equal Justice Initiative, who said you're better off being rich and guilty than poor and innocent.

"I couldn't not have done this," Newsom said. "There was an easy out, but ... I would the rest of my life felt, you know, ashamed of myself."

Commuting the death sentences of all 548 state prisoners awaiting execution pushes the bounds of his authority once again. California voters have twice rejected ballot measures to abolish the death penalty , first in 2012 and again in 2016, and Newsom's decision overrides the will of the courts and state laws that permit capital punishment.

Under the state Constitution, Newsom has the power to commute about 40% of the death sentences on his own. The rest of the cases, which involve prisoners who had a felony conviction on their record prior to receiving a death sentence, or racked up additional crimes while awaiting execution, require approval from the California Supreme Court — a constitutional check to ensure the governor's actions are not an abuse of power.

The court rejected 10 commutations handed out by Gov. Jerry Brown in his last full month in office — all of which involved people convicted of multiple felonies — and did not provide an explanation for the action.

Despite Newsom's push to commute all death sentences, capital punishment remains legal in California and prosecutors can continue seeking that punishment.

Los Angeles County Dist. Atty. Nathan Hochman said until the law is changed, his office "will continue to evaluate every death penalty-eligible case with the rigor, care and restraint these decisions demand."

Sacramento County Sheriff Jim Cooper urged Newsom to reconsider the commutations.

He said he remembers watching Luis Bracamontes, who was sentenced to death for killing Sacramento County Sheriff's Deputy Danny Oliver and Placer County Sheriff's Detective Michael Davis Jr. in 2014, "laugh in court while their families, including Danny's two young daughters, had to sit and watch.

"Deputy Danny Oliver and Detective Michael Davis Jr. should be alive today, enjoying long and healthy lives with their families," Cooper said in a statement. "Instead, the man who murdered them has now escaped his sentence."

Others accused the governor of reducing the death penalty sentences to seek an advantage in the 2028 presidential election.

"The people of California deserve leaders who put politics and personal ambition aside and pursue truth, accountability, and justice with courage, integrity, and transparency," said Michael Hestrin, Riverside County district attorney, in a statement. "Instead they have been presented with a decision that demonstrates a profound disregard for the victims, their families, and the prosecutors who dedicated themselves to seeking justice on their behalf."

A poll conducted in August by the Pew Research Center found that about two-thirds of voters nationally favor the death penalty for people convicted of murder.

Political analysts suggest that reducing the sentences adds to Newsom's credentials as a progressive leader and aligns him with Democratic primary voters on the issue if he runs for president. Republicans, however, could take advantage of Newsom's action and cast him as a soft-on-crime liberal who is out of touch with most Americans, which risks turning away moderate voters.

But others cautioned that national political elections are hard to predict.

Gar Culbert, chair of the political science department at Cal State Los Angeles, said it would be politically advantageous for Newsom to try to appeal to the Democratic Party's base as he considers a run for president. Culbert said he doesn't believe the death penalty will be a substantial issue in a general election when, if Newsom becomes the Democratic presidential nominee, his Republican challenger would attack his record as California governor regardless.

"It's possible he's not being strategic," Culbert said. "Maybe he doesn't have to be strategic because he just might think it's the right thing to do."

The governor first issued a moratorium on executions about two months after he took office in 2019, saying capital punishment is discriminatory and unjust. Without the moratorium, 45 people would be subject to execution now, according to his office.

Daniel Zingale worked for Newsom as a senior advisor in the governor's office at the start of his first term. Part of Zingale's job at the time was to consider how the governor's actions would be received by the public.

"The only piece of data he was not interested in in that process were the polls," Zingale said. "His view, and I agree with this, is this is not an issue that you can leverage politically."

Newsom's decision to commute the sentences won't have much practical effect in a state that has not executed a prisoner since 2006. At Newsom's command, the death chamber was dismantled at San Quentin State Prison, now San Quentin Rehabilitation Center, after he issued his moratorium.

His successor, Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, has also said he will continue the pause on executions.

There was no immediate need to offer commutations to save the lives of the inmates.

Taking no action would have been the safe bet, Newsom said in an interview about his decision a day after he made the announcement. Many people around him, he said, advised him to do nothing.

He also understands that commuting the sentences could make him vulnerable if he runs for president.

"I'm not an idiot. The ads write themselves," Newsom said. "But I just also would be fake. I wouldn't be myself and if I'm going to be up there and not be myself, I couldn't do that."

With the clock ticking on his time in office, the governor said he also doesn't want to leave with regrets.

"I don't want to be one of the elders on some panel talking about what I would have, could have, should have done," Newsom said. "I've spent my life trying not to be that person. I've been willing to take risks. I've been willing to go first on so many issues.

"If others aren't willing to do it, you know what? I'll raise my hand, and I'm happy, honestly, to take the hits."

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .
