articles.title: Texas mayor instructs police to limit co-operation with ICE
articles.summary: There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work.
articles.body:
The mayor of Houston, Texas, has directed the city's police to limit co-operation with federal immigration officials.

The move by John Whitmire, a Democrat, comes on the heels of stunning victories by the party in Texas during this week's midterm elections. It breaks with policy set by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid.

"I do this to begin a healing process," Whitmire said on Friday, and to "reduce fear and anxiety across our community". He added: "I also do this knowing that elections matter."

There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work.

Houston police chief Noe Diaz said on Friday that officers will now only contact ICE if someone they arrest for a jailable offence also has an administrative ICE warrant, which are issued internally by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), within which ICE operates.

"For example, if our police officers pull someone over for a minor traffic infraction and they write a citation, that person receives a citation and goes about their day," Diaz said.

Under the previous rules, Houston police officers were required to inform ICE if anyone they were dealing with came up as having one of these warrants attached to their name when they were searched on the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) - a digital database that includes records on wanted persons, stolen property, certain missing people and those arrested and fingerprinted for serious offences.

Whitmire said on Friday that he had directed the Houston Police Department to make the changes through an executive order.

He also called on Congress to change federal immigration rules, saying "ICE needs better training. They need body cameras. They need to be trained in de-escalation."

He added, "But this can only be done in Washington. I can only control what I can control."

Five ways Trump has changed immigration in the US

In response, a spokesperson for the DHS told Houston's NBC affiliate, KPRC 2, in a statement: "We remain disappointed that sanctuary politicians seek to limit cooperation with ICE, as our law enforcement are simply fulfilling their sworn duties to serve and protect our communities."

"Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country," the spokesperson added.

Another Texas city, Austin, has also begun implementing a similar policy change.

Democrats won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.

Texas, a long-time Republican stronghold, was the site of one of the most stunning upsets in the vote, with the state electing its first Latina governor, Gina Hinojosa, as the first Democrat governor since 1995. It also elected its first Democratic senator since 1988.

Whitmire has previously faced criticism for abiding by immigration enforcement policies under the Trump administration.

Abbott has also threatened to take pull millions in funds from cities like Houston, Dallas and Austin unless they allow police to cooperate fully with federal immigration officials.

The BBC has contacted Abbott's office for comment.

Whitmire's announcement comes a week after an ICE officer was charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after he allegedly hit a man with a vehicle in Texas.

Earlier this year, large protests broke out in Houston after an ICE officer fatally shot a man driving to work.

The deceased, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Mexican national who lived in the US as an undocumented immigrant for decades, was not the intended target, officials said after the incident.

articles.body:
Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) blasted President Trump’s Friday decision to replace outgoing White House chief of staff Susie Wiles with top adviser Stephen Miller, saying the president “needs to rethink” his decision.

“I’ve criticized a lot of the president’s advisors for bad advice that I think … created some of the environment on Tuesday, but the president made this decision, and the president needs to rethink it,” Tillis told CNN’s Jake Tapper Friday.

“It is a colossal mistake, and the last thing we need 72 hours after the a– whooping we got on Tuesday,” he added.

Wiles’s replacement is the first major White House shakeup since Republicans’ rocky midterm performance , losing at least seven Senate seats and 42 House seats as of Friday — with several races still outstanding.

Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement tactics, which Miller architected, contributed to the president’s approval rating hitting a career low ahead of Election Day — likely impacting the GOP’s performance. One especially contentious operation at the start of 2026 took place in Minneapolis, during which two U.S. citizens were fatally shot by federal agents. At the time, Miller referred to the victims as domestic terrorists .

“This past Tuesday, Republicans lost because we lost the narrative on the border, a success that the president should have been heralding,” Tillis said. “Now we’re talking about putting one of the most partisan, polarizing figures, and not only polarizing in terms of Republicans and Democrats, but even among Republicans.”

Just after the election night, Trump reportedly told aides Miller’s immigration campaign had gone too far, according to The Wall Street Journal. Tillis said it “doesn’t make sense” why Trump would promote Miller if he thought immigration had become a political liability.

“What was inappropriate is to take a guy who made us lose on the immigration issue,” Tillis said. “So no, he doesn’t get a passing grade for me, even judging on the kind of curve that I made with some people among his advisers.”

The GOP senator is frequent critic of some of Trump’s cabinet and other advisers. In March, he erupted at then Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in hearing, saying he was “disappointed” in her job performance.

In a viral post back in January, Tillis also compared Noem and Miller to “sycophants.”

The North Carolina Republican announced he would not run for reelection this year, and Gov. Roy Cooper (D-N.C.) won the open seat to replace him by nearly 20 points. The blue wave hit the Tar Heel State as hard as any Tuesday night; Democrats flipped five of its congressional seats, with five races still outstanding, according to Decision Desk HQ.

articles.title: After Trump's midterm rout, Europe sees cracks in populist right. It may not stop France’s Le Pen
articles.summary: President Donald Trump ’s victory sent a populist shock wave across the West. Now, Europe is asking whether the midterm rout of his Republican Party will sen...
articles.body:
PARIS (AP) — A decade ago, U.S. President Donald Trump 's victory sent a populist shock wave across the West. Now, Europe is asking whether the midterm rout of his Republican Party will send one back.

European opponents of right-wing populism see the U.S. vote as the latest sign of its faltering advance. Since April, voters have ousted Hungary's Viktor Orbán , ended Aleksandar Vučić's long grip on Serbia and blocked the Bolsonaro family's return in Brazil.

"When cracks in power become more visible, this can trigger a cascade effect," said Péter Krekó, director of Budapest's Political Capital Institute.

Nowhere would such a cascade matter more than in France, where nationalist Marine Le Pen is the front-runner in a presidential election six months away that could put the European Union's only nuclear arsenal, and a U.N. Security Council veto, in far-right hands.

The populist right's recent defeats could rattle the woman vying to become France's first Madame la Présidente. But the anger punishing populists in power from Budapest to Belgrade could carry her to it — precisely because her National Rally party has never governed France.

Le Pen also faces a legal cliffhanger. France's highest court aims to rule on her appeal against an embezzlement conviction by early April, just weeks before the first round of voting; if it rules against her, she could campaign and face voters wearing an electronic tag.

"She could still be barred from running, and now Americans delivered this sort of rebuke to Trump's kind of populism," said Carmen Artaza, 31, a Paris resident educated in the United States. "That's bound to rattle her — unsettle her campaign."

But in France, "the far right still has the wind in its sails," said Sciences Po political scientist Gilles Ivaldi.

Analysts say voters who handed Democrats control of the U.S. House and Senate may have punished Trump's record, especially on the economy , more than his "America First" ideas.

Populists are still winning some elections, too: Such candidates have taken presidencies in Poland, Chile and Colombia since mid-2025.

"The trend toward the far right has been the defining feature of 21st-century politics," said Daphne Halikiopoulou, a politics professor at Britain's University of York.

But lately, defeats for the illiberal populist camp have been piling up.

"The midterms are a very favorable result for the center left, and this could hinder the far right," she said.

Leaders or parties espousing nationalist, anti-immigration policies have suffered at least eight national election setbacks in roughly 18 months: in Romania, the Netherlands, Portugal, Hungary, Sweden, Serbia, Brazil and now the United States.

And many were emphatic: Portugal elected moderate Socialist António José Seguro over hard-right populist André Ventura by two to one; Hungary ended Orbán's 16 years in power; Serbia's Vučić conceded defeat last month to a student-led protest movement; and Romania chose pro-European centrist Nicușor Dan over nationalist George Simion.

Last month, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva narrowly beat Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.

Other votes thinned the ranks of anti-immigration parties. Geert Wilders' party lost 11 seats in the Netherlands as the centrist party surged. In Sweden, the hard-right Sweden Democrats lost 11 seats as the left-leaning opposition won a narrow majority.

The results "show clearly that far-right politics are not popular," said Aurélien Mondon, a politics expert at Britain's University of Bath.

Even some on the populist right see a pattern. The U.S. midterms "join the defeats of Bolsonaro and Orbán," Markus Frohnmaier, a senior lawmaker with the far-right AfD, wrote on X.

Each defeat can make the next one easier to imagine. Voters need to believe that "an increasingly authoritarian regime with vast resources can be defeated," Krekó said. "The midterm results helped create that sense."

The French left seized on the result, while the far right gave it a Gallic shrug.

"There is no inevitability in politics," said Raphaël Glucksmann, the French center-left presidential candidate, calling it "a message of hope for all."

The National Rally, which cheered Trump's return to power last year, is now keeping him at arm's length.

"What happens in other countries is none of my business," party president Jordan Bardella told RTL radio.

Sébastien Chenu, who leads the far-right party's lawmakers in the National Assembly, called the vote "a rejection of Donald Trump's policies" in a statement to The Associated Press, blaming inflation and fuel prices driven by a war with Iran "that he himself started."

In Germany, AfD co-leader Alice Weidel blamed "the disastrous consequences of the Iran war."

The message from Europe's nationalists: The defeat was Trump's, not theirs.

After three failed bids, Le Pen has never looked stronger, according to French pollsters.

Yet the race to be her main challenger is wide open, with hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, center-right former Prime Minister Édouard Philippe and Glucksmann among the contenders.

"Losing an election is definitely a sign of decline. But it's not sudden death," Halikiopoulou said. "In many cases, far-right parties are losing because their competitors are adopting their positions."

In Britain, Labour hardened its stance on immigration, especially under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, to fend off Nigel Farage's Reform UK.

In France, the Senate last week approved a bill from President Emmanuel Macron's government that could make anyone who knowingly joins a violent group pay up to 10,000 euros ($11,200) for what others destroy, and let the state dock family benefits to cover it — long a Le Pen idea.

The real danger, Mondon said, is "the failure of the mainstream elite" to counter the far right. A decade under Macron has brought "the mainstreaming of far-right talking points."

Le Pen's advantage: She has never governed

For Le Pen, the lesson of the midterms may be less that populists lose than that incumbents do.

Anger at incumbents has been building for years. In 2024, for the first time since records began, every governing party that faced a national election in a developed country lost vote share, according to ParlGov, a University of Bremen database.

The far right is rising where it sits in opposition and centrists rule, as in France, Austria and Germany, where the AfD took a record 43.8% in Saxony-Anhalt's state election in September.

Anger and a hunger for radical change, embodied by both Le Pen and Mélenchon, now dominate French politics, Ivaldi said.

The election will show whether there is "still a barrier against the far-right," he said. Voters across the political spectrum rallied behind Macron to block her in 2017 and 2022.

For now, he said, France "could well experience its own 'Trump moment,' like the U.S. in 2016."

Voters have shown they can turn populists out of power. France will show whether they can keep one from winning it.

Halikiopoulou put it simply: "Were the midterms a massive blow to Trump? Yes. Were they important? Absolutely. But the fact remains that Trump is still in power."

Associated Press writer Geir Moulson in Berlin contributed to this report.

articles.title: After their midterm win and Stephen Miller’s promotion, Democrats gear up for a fight on immigration
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — After Democrats' overwhelming midterm victories this week, winning candidates spoke of the need, once they are sworn in, to rein in Preside...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — After Democrats' overwhelming midterm victories this week, winning candidates spoke of the need, once they are sworn in, to rein in President Donald Trump's mass deportation machine . Some suggested putting forward a new vision for immigration reform while both houses of Congress are in Democratic control.

The lofty goals come after two years in which Democrats, while in the minority, were limited in how much they could counter Trump's supercharged and, at times, chaotic immigration enforcement. But there are clear limits to what they can achieve even after Democrats' epic win, with Trump — who rode into power in part on a promise to curb immigration — in office for another two years and wielding his veto power.

What's more, Republicans have frontloaded billions of dollars for immigration enforcement. And the key architect of the president's hard-line immigration agenda, Stephen Miller, was elevated Friday to become Trump's chief of staff — suggesting immigration enforcement may not slow down any time soon.

Here's a look at what might come next for immigration after Election Day:

Investigating alleged corruption and ICE policies

Democrats appear ready to use the power of congressional oversight to investigate Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security. That strategy will likely resonate with voters angry aboutt how enforcement operations were carried out in places like Minneapolis or ICE arrests of longtime immigrants integrated into American society.

The administration ramped up immigration enforcement during the first two years of Trump's second term, launching major operations in multiple cities and sending arrests soaring . DHS also came under criticism for alleged corruption and misuse of funds it was granted to carry out Trump's immigration agenda.

Nationally, about 6 in 10 voters said the Trump administration's actions on immigration enforcement had "gone too far," according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters. A similar share disapproved of how ICE was doing its job. And about 6 in 10 voters said immigrants to the U.S. today do more to "help the country," while less than half, about 4 in 10, said they do more to "hurt the country."

Rep. Robert Garcia, a Los Angeles-area Democrat who will take over the House Oversight Committee and is a prominent critic of Trump's immigration agenda, warned the administration to "lawyer up," adding that investigating alleged abuses at DHS was one of his priorities.

The next Congress will "address the Trump administration's assault on the rule of law and hold those responsible accountable," said Mississippi Rep. Bennie Thompson, the ranking Democrat on the House Homeland Security committee.

Those investigations could delve into issues like DHS purchases of massive warehouses to hold arrested immigrants; whether ICE cut corners when hiring thousands of new deportation officers; or deaths in ICE detention facilities.

Garcia and Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut held shadow hearings featuring family members of people killed during immigration enforcement operations, a whistleblower exposing problems with ICE training, and American citizens caught up in immigration enforcement operations.

No Republicans attended and Democrats couldn't subpoena witnesses. Now they can, opening up a new level of scrutiny of the administration's actions.

Calls to put forward a Democratic vision for immigration

The last time Congress even came close to passing comprehensive immigration reform was in 2013. That proposal cleared the Senate but died in the House.

Border crossings that surged under the Biden administration further served to dampen any Democratic enthusiasm to talk about legalization for any immigrants.

Sarah Pierce, director of social policy for Third Way, a Washington, D.C., think tank, said Democrats need to show voters their own vision for immigration and border security and not just focus on oversight hearings of what happened during the last two years.

"They should lean into oversight, but I think that they also need to couple that with a proactive vision for what immigration should look like in the United States," said Pierce.

At least one of the party's new senators is ready for the discussion. During an interview with Fox News after the election, Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas discussed the need to pass comprehensive immigration reform, including a pathway to citizenship for immigrants living and working illegally in the country for years.

In the House, Rep. Gabe Vasquez of New Mexico pointed to the Democratic gains made with Latino voters and the higher numbers of Latino lawmakers who will take office next year as reasons for Democrats to not shy away from talking about immigration issues.

He said Democrats should find ways to address immigration through a lens of affordability, a central issue for voters. For example, they could tackle staffing shortages by creating a new visa class for workers who provide care for children or the elderly.

"This cannot be a third-rail issue for Democrats," said Vasquez. "We can actually reform our immigration system to bring costs down for all Americans and at the same time give people who are either here undocumented or want to come to this country an opportunity to have legal status."

Democrats' power to curb Trump's immigration agenda is limited

Trump, shortly after the election, said he was prepared to work with Democrats on certain issues, highlighting immigration as one of them. But that collaborative tone may not bear out in practice.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin vowed on social media, "Deportations will continue." A few days later, Trump promoted Miller to become his chief of staff.

Immigration and Latino activists lambasted Miller's promotion, calling it an act of defiance after voters spoke clearly at the polls and a sign the president would continue his immigration policies. California's Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla, who's been a key critic of Trump's immigration agenda, said Trump was choosing to double down by picking Miller and vowed, "So will we."

It's unclear if Democrats and the White House will find a middle ground to successfully pass immigration legislation. With Trump in office for another two years, he can veto any Democratic legislation, and Republicans have the money and the personnel to pursue Trump's immigration agenda regardless of Tuesday's results.

Republicans during the summer of 2025 supercharged immigration enforcement with $150 billion intended to expand immigration detention capacity, finish the border wall and hire thousands more deportation officers. Earlier this year they frontloaded routine funding for ICE and Border Patrol for the next three years.

"My fear is that enforcement will get worse. And the country will also see that Congress does not have many tools to stop the executive branch because the executive branch power on immigration has grown so vast," said Andrea Flores, who was a policy adviser in the Obama and Biden administrations.

Conservatives want action from lame duck Congress

Many administration supporters want this current Congress — in the little time it has left — to pass laws solidifying the gains the Trump administration says it has made on border security and immigration. Without codifying changes to asylum law or tightening requirements on employers to verify workers' immigration status, they warn, a different administration could quickly reverse the new immigration landscape Trump has shaped.

NumbersUSA, an advocacy group that seeks to restrict immigration, has a timer on its website counting down the days until this Congress is over with a warning to "make border security permanent."

"If this Congress in the lame duck does not secure the border with lasting legislation," said the organization's co-president, Jeremy Beck, "then this Congress will have failed to meet the moment."

Associated Press reporter Linley Sanders contributed to this report.

articles.title: DeSantis blasts Washington Post over report he's preparing 2028 presidential bid
articles.summary: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis accused The Washington Post of fabricating claims he reached out to political consultants about a potential 2028 presidential bid.
articles.body: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis fired back Friday at a report that he is preparing another White House bid in 2028, accusing The Washington Post of fabricating claims that he has started reaching out to political consultants about a potential campaign. "The Washington Post is fabricating this out of whole cloth," DeSantis wrote on X. "I have not reached out to anybody about running for anything." "Just another pathetic attempt to garner clicks. Using anonymous sources of course!" he added. The Post reported Friday, citing three people briefed on his plans, that DeSantis was preparing to seek the Republican presidential nomination in 2028. VANCE, CRUZ AND DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS BATTLE OVER PARTY'S FUTURE BEGINS The newspaper reported that DeSantis, who unsuccessfully ran for president in 2024 and is term-limited after 2026, had already reached out to at least one national political consultant about working on a prospective campaign. A federal super PAC tied to DeSantis also sent out a fundraising text earlier this week, The Post reported. DeSantis continued pushing back against the report in exchanges with social media users. When one user expressed hope that The Post's reporting was accurate, the governor replied that he was "sorry to disappoint." DeSantis also responded to another user who suggested political consultants may have been using his name to attract attention. "Probably the case. But maybe just made up by WaPo," he wrote. FIRST MUSLIM SENATOR, FIRST BLACK FEMALE GOVERNOR: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTION RESULTS MAKE HISTORY Speculation surrounding DeSantis' political future comes just days after Republicans suffered sweeping defeats in the midterm elections, losing control of both chambers of Congress and several traditionally Republican strongholds. The Sunshine State, however, remained a bright spot for the GOP, with Republican Byron Donalds winning the governor's race. "This is close to an extinction-level event for Republicans," DeSantis said Wednesday, warning that among the nation's 10 most populous states, Florida would be the only one with Republican control of its government. DESANTIS CALLS GOP MIDTERM LOSSES 'EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT' — AND EXPLAINS WHY FLORIDA SURVIVED DeSantis previously sought the 2024 Republican presidential nomination but suspended his campaign in January 2024 after the Iowa caucuses and endorsed Donald Trump. The governor, who will leave office in January, has previously left open the possibility of another presidential campaign. articles.title: Do not investigate Trump’s corporate allies until he leaves office
articles.summary: The US presidential pardon power has created a constitutional absurdity that can protect those accused of corruption.
articles.body:
In a functioning constitutional democracy, allegations of corporate corruption would ordinarily invite immediate investigation. Congress would demand documents, summon executives and expose wrongdoing to public scrutiny.

With Democrats having won control of both houses of Congress, the expectation will be that they exercise these oversight powers vigorously. In Donald Trump’s America, however, there is a compelling argument for doing precisely the opposite.

If the objective is criminal accountability rather than political theatre, the incoming Democratic majorities might be better advised to preserve the evidence but postpone public congressional investigations and disclosures concerning potential criminal wrongdoing by Trump’s corporate allies until he leaves office in January 2029, thereby avoiding the possibility of presidential pardons that could place those responsible beyond the reach of federal criminal prosecution.

This may sound absurd, but it follows from the extraordinary breadth of the presidential pardon power. Under the US Constitution, a president may pardon individuals for federal crimes before they have been charged, investigated or convicted. What was conceived as an exceptional power of mercy can become an instrument for protecting political associates, wealthy benefactors and corporate executives from criminal accountability.

A Washington Post investigation published on October 26 reveals that powerful technology and defence companies that cultivated close relationships with Trump are increasingly anxious about the prospect of a Democratic Congress. Companies including Palantir, Anduril, OpenAI and Meta face possible congressional scrutiny over government contracts, political contributions and their relationships with the administration. Some executives are reportedly scrambling to establish relationships with Democratic politicians as the prospect of congressional investigations approaches.

The financial stakes are considerable. The Post reports that 15 companies backed by Trump’s sons received $3.2bn in federal contracts, investments and loans, most after Trump returned to the White House. Congressional Democrats have raised questions about potential conflicts of interest and whether politically connected companies received preferential treatment. These relationships provide legitimate grounds for investigating how public resources were allocated.

Ordinarily, such investigations would be welcomed as an essential exercise of congressional oversight. But consider what might happen if congressional hearings uncovered evidence of fraud, bribery or corruption. The findings could identify those responsible and establish compelling evidence of criminal misconduct. Trump could then issue sweeping pardons protecting the individuals concerned from federal prosecution. Investigators might succeed in exposing wrongdoing only to discover that their efforts had furnished the president with a list of people to protect.

Trump’s record provides ample reason to take this possibility seriously. His official clemency record includes pardons for individuals convicted of securities fraud, wire fraud and other financial offences. In March 2025, he pardoned Trevor Milton, the founder of electric-truck manufacturer Nikola, who had been convicted of defrauding investors. He also pardoned HDR Global Trading Limited, the corporate entity associated with the cryptocurrency exchange BitMEX. The crypto firm had pleaded guilty to violating the Bank Secrecy Act. Several individuals associated with the company also received pardons.

The pardon of HDR Global Trading deserves particular attention. Trump extended clemency not only to company executives but to the corporation itself, which had pleaded guilty to a federal offence. The consequences for corporate accountability in an era of enormous corporate wealth and political influence deserve far greater attention than they have received.

The Supreme Court laid the groundwork for this extraordinary authority in Ex parte Garland (1866). The Court interpreted the pardon power as extending to federal offences after their commission, regardless of whether criminal proceedings had commenced. Congress could not impose ordinary legislative restrictions on its exercise. The ruling effectively recognised the president’s authority to forgive federal crimes without waiting for the criminal justice system to establish guilt.

The implications are staggering. An executive might have committed fraud involving millions of dollars, or a government contractor might have secured contracts through bribery. If those offences fall within federal criminal jurisdiction, a sufficiently broad presidential pardon can extinguish criminal liability for the covered conduct. Presidential pardons cannot authorise future crimes, prevent state prosecutions or generally extinguish civil liability. Nor do they prevent congressional investigations. But the elimination of federal criminal punishment for past offences is consequential enough.

This is not simply a Trump problem. Joe Biden demonstrated the extraordinary reach of the same constitutional power when he issued a sweeping pardon to his son Hunter Biden in December 2024. The pardon covered federal offences committed or potentially committed over almost 11 years, extending far beyond the specific charges on which Hunter Biden had been prosecuted or convicted.

In his final hours in office, Biden went further, issuing preemptive pardons to members of his family and several public figures, including Anthony Fauci, retired General Mark Milley and individuals associated with the congressional investigation into the January 6 attack. Biden justified these measures as necessary protection against politically motivated prosecutions by the incoming Trump administration. His stated motivations differed from protecting corporate financial misconduct, and the pardons did not establish wrongdoing by their recipients. Nevertheless, his actions demonstrated how easily the power could be used to shield selected individuals from federal criminal proceedings without any independent determination that clemency was warranted.

The precedent should trouble Americans regardless of their political loyalties. Biden’s supporters may regard his actions as justified protection against threatened political retribution. Trump can invoke the same constitutional authority for entirely different purposes. The central difficulty is that the legal power does not depend upon the president’s motives being honourable, the beneficiaries being deserving or the public interest being served.

This brings us back to the peculiar dilemma facing congressional Democrats. Why assemble and publicise evidence of alleged criminal misconduct while the president retains the authority to pardon those implicated? Why identify potential defendants and present the allegations against them before the administration leaves office? Trump might issue preemptive pardons regardless. Indeed, he has already signalled his willingness to do so, declaring in a November 2 interview that he would protect Elon Musk and other allies facing Democratic investigations and grant pardons if necessary. A detailed congressional investigation could therefore provide him with a convenient inventory of possible beneficiaries.

This is not an argument for destroying evidence, suppressing whistleblowers or preventing investigations necessary to stop ongoing illegality. Records must be preserved, relevant limitation periods protected and unlawful practices halted. State authorities must remain free to exercise their independent jurisdiction. The narrower argument concerns the timing of public congressional disclosures that could frustrate eventual federal prosecutions. Even that limited postponement carries costs for transparency and democratic oversight.

The objection is obvious. Citizens are entitled to know whether public money has been misused and whether government contracts have been awarded improperly. Delaying disclosure may permit wrongdoing to continue, allow witnesses to disappear or give those implicated additional opportunities to conceal evidence. These are serious concerns that cannot simply be brushed aside. Yet the fact that withholding potentially incriminating findings must even be considered as a means of preserving criminal accountability exposes a troubling defect in the constitutional system.

The US Constitution is almost 240 years old. It requires fundamental reform in several respects, but few provisions illustrate the urgency more clearly than the presidential pardon power. The framers entrusted this authority to a single individual in the expectation that it would be exercised with wisdom and restraint. They could scarcely have anticipated an era in which vast corporate fortunes, political patronage and presidential power would become so closely intertwined.

The Constitution should be amended to establish meaningful limits on presidential clemency. Pardons involving the president’s family, personal financial interests or political associates implicated in misconduct connected to the administration should be subject to strict constitutional safeguards. Sweeping preemptive pardons covering years of unspecified criminal conduct also deserve reconsideration. An independent clemency commission, operating under constitutionally prescribed standards, could provide scrutiny of controversial pardons without eliminating the legitimate humanitarian purposes of executive mercy.

Such reforms would require constitutional amendment. The Supreme Court has interpreted the existing pardon power so expansively that ordinary legislation cannot simply curtail it. Article V makes constitutional change exceptionally difficult, but difficulty cannot justify preserving a power susceptible to serious abuse merely because it has existed for more than two centuries.

There are compelling reasons to retain presidential clemency. Criminal justice systems make mistakes, sentences can be excessive, and mercy has an important place in the justice system. But mercy must not become a privilege reserved for the politically connected, or a mechanism through which presidents protect their associates from the consequences of criminal misconduct.

For now, the perverse logic of the system suggests that those seeking meaningful federal criminal accountability might be wiser to postpone public exposure of potential offences until Trump leaves office. It is an astonishing proposition for a country that prides itself on the rule of law. A constitutional system in which exposing corruption can become the means of protecting those responsible is badly in need of repair.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: American war hero details dire living conditions US troops face as Hegseth taps him to 'fix' it
articles.summary: Dakota Meyer reveals troops going a year without hot water and sleeping in cars as he tours military barracks on Pete Hegseth's Pentagon mission.
articles.body: Some troops have gone a year without hot water. Others are sleeping in their cars to escape barracks without air conditioning. And some are asking for little more than drywall, spackle and paint so they can make repairs themselves. Those are among the conditions Medal of Honor recipient Dakota Meyer says he has encountered while touring military installations on a mission from War Secretary Pete Hegseth: Fix a barracks system plagued by decades of neglect. "I would tell you that there's only a couple that I've seen that are good," Meyer told Fox News Digital in an interview Thursday. Meyer, who serves as senior adviser to the Pentagon's Barracks Task Force, has visited more than eight installations across the Army, Navy, Air Force and Marine Corps since taking on the assignment and plans to visit 30 before the end of the year. "What I thought was gonna be a professional job very quickly turned into personal," Meyer said. DAKOTA MEYER TALKS SERVICE, BLASTS CONTROVERSIAL DESIGN FOR GLOBAL WAR ON TERROR MEMORIAL At one installation, Meyer recalled asking a 19-year-old service member what she would change about her living conditions if she could "wave a magic wand." "If she could just have a hot shower," Meyer recalled. "It's absolutely heartbreaking." The Pentagon's barracks problems long predate Hegseth and have survived repeated attempts at reform. A sweeping 2023 Government Accountability Office investigation documented serious health and safety hazards and found that the department lacked reliable information about the condition of its own barracks, could not determine how much of its facilities spending went toward them and provided insufficient oversight. Congress and the military services have since committed billions toward improvements, including initiatives ranging from the Marine Corps' "Barracks 2030" to a Navy overhaul of unaccompanied housing. Yet serious problems persist. As of this year, 12 of GAO's 31 recommendations remained outstanding. Hegseth has sought to centralize the effort under a department-wide task force and accelerate improvements, with Meyer saying the secretary has made clear that identifying problems is no longer enough. "The secretary has made it clear to me he doesn't expect me to observe this, study it, or to make it better. He expects me to fix it," Meyer said. "And that's exactly what we're going to do." Meyer, the only Medal of Honor hero to reenlist after receiving the award, said one of his first requests was for Hegseth to give the task force an "authoritative role," rather than simply create another layer of oversight. The goal, he said, was to give the team the ability "to go out and make decisions, to be able to have impact, to be able to make change, and to be able to direct where that funding goes and how fast it gets to our service members." EXCLUSIVE: HEGSETH TO DOUBLE CUTS TO GENERALS, ADMIRALS IN MAJOR PENTAGON SHAKEUP Meyer argued the problem is not simply a lack of money. Funding shortfalls, continuing resolutions and years of deferred maintenance have all contributed, he said, but so have layers of contracting rules and bureaucracy that can slow even relatively basic repairs. A separate watchdog review found the Pentagon facing a $285 billion maintenance backlog across its broader military facilities' portfolio, underscoring the scale of the department's infrastructure challenges. "When you look at the contracting aspect, it's easier for people to say no," Meyer said. Funding is also part of the problem, according to Meyer, who pointed to Congress' failure to enact full-year defense appropriations for fiscal 2027. The Pentagon is currently operating under a continuing resolution through Dec. 11, which generally funds ongoing programs at prior-year rates while lawmakers negotiate a broader spending package. "When you can't get a budget, when you're waiting on Congress to pass a budget, to be able to get the funding there, I mean, that is a huge issue," Meyer said. But he also argued that the Pentagon has too often measured progress by how much money has been obligated or put under contract, rather than whether troops actually see improvements in their living conditions. "Our service members don't, they don't live in our budget lines," Meyer said. "They live in the rooms that those budget lines are there to impact." For Meyer, that has meant getting out of Washington and hearing directly from the troops living with the consequences. "You can't fix these problems or understand these problems by standing on the carpet of the Pentagon," he said. "You've got to go out there and talk to these service members." What he has heard, Meyer said, is striking partly because of how little troops are asking for. "They're asking for a hot shower. They're asking for a place to wash their clothes. They're asking for a door that locks. They're asking to be able to go to sleep in a place that doesn't have mold. I mean, they're asking for light bulbs." "They're willing to be part of the solution," he added. Meyer stopped short of placing the blame solely on installation commanders, saying many want to improve conditions but have been constrained by a system that has normalized poor barracks for years. "I think this is a multidimensional problem, and it's complex," he said. "I think that you have commanders out there that want to take care of their service members. I've seen that across the board. But ... they still have to have the ability to do that." Meyer was far less forgiving of previous Pentagon leadership, arguing that years of investments and reform initiatives had failed to translate into adequate living conditions for troops. "Don't kid yourself," Meyer said. "In the past ... it wasn't a priority to the leadership." Previous administrations and military leaders did launch barracks improvement efforts and devoted billions of dollars to construction, renovation and maintenance, even as government watchdogs continued to document serious deficiencies. Meyer said Hegseth has made the issue a personal priority. "We have the Secretary of War who is putting people first, and he's not just saying that, he's doing it through his actions," Meyer said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Meyer has put his own name on whether the latest effort succeeds, saying previously that if the barracks aren't fixed, there is "only one person to blame" — himself. Asked what "fixed" would actually look like, Meyer offered a simpler standard than any Pentagon metric. "People are living in places that I would be okay for my daughters living in," he said.

articles.title: Trump sends ‘clear message’ to Democrats with Miller promotion
articles.summary: President Trump sent a blunt message to the incoming Democratic majority on Capitol Hill by tapping Stephen Miller to be his new chief of staff, setting up what is likely to be a contentious two years between both ends of Pennsylvania Avenue. Miller is loathed by most Democrats, many of whom view him as xenophobic…
articles.body:
President Trump sent a blunt message to the incoming Democratic majority on Capitol Hill by tapping Stephen Miller to be his new chief of staff , setting up what is likely to be a contentious two years between both ends of Pennsylvania Avenue.

Miller is loathed by most Democrats , many of whom view him as xenophobic and racist. Additionally, the incoming chief of staff is not known to compromise with the other side of the aisle, preferring a combative approach to pushing the Trump agenda.

Many see the move as Trump signaling to congressional Democrats that he is not thinking about compromise and will implement his agenda through executive authority.

“They are not going to slow down on executive power, executive orders, and regulations,” said Joe Grogan, former director of Trump’s Domestic Policy Council in his first administration and senior adviser at Covington & Burling LLP. “Stephen is going to move aggressively on all of that.”

Mick Mulvaney, who was Trump’s chief of staff during his first term, said the president’s pick of Miller sends “a clear message.”

“The White House will continue to prioritize executive authority in the next two years,” Mulvaney told The Hill.

“Stephen is a good choice on many levels, but face it, if the president was looking to build bridges with the new incoming Democrat majorities, he would probably have gone in a different direction,” he continued.

Not everyone in Trump’s orbit and the broader GOP universe is thrilled about the decision.

“We’re cooked,” said one former Trump administration official. “It’s exactly the opposite direction voters are begging Republicans to go. Susie was the best thing that happened to President Trump,” the former official continued, referencing chief of staff Susie Wiles, who resigned Friday.

Another former Trump White House official who worked with Miller described the incoming chief of staff as “smart and opinionated, but does not have many close friends on the White House staff.”

“Most of his colleagues view him as somewhat of an arrogant lone wolf,” the former official said.

“Trump likes him because he’s been a hard-liner on immigration enforcement in both his terms, but Trump has also gone against Miller when his ‘no holds barred’ approach goes too far like in Minneapolis earlier this year,” they added.

The violent optics of the clashes between federal immigration enforcement and protesters in Minnesota earlier this year led, in part, to the ouster of former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem. Border Patrol officer Gregory Bovino, who served as commander at large of the law enforcement arm, was also removed from his position following the unrest.

However, Miller, who strongly defended the operation, kept his role in the administration.

His promotion comes after the president said Wednesday that he would “probably get along with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive, adding that he wields “the power of the veto.”

“They’ve already called, and they want to talk about things, and that’s fine,” the president said.

Democrats, however, say Trump’s promotion of Miller has thrown that possibility out the window.

“Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said in a post on the social platform X. “His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor.”

“Fire him today,” added Jeffries, who is likely to be the next House Speaker.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) responded to Miller’s promotion by saying Trump has “learned nothing from his historic defeat.”

“Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice,” Schumer wrote on X. “Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way.”

One Republican lobbyist warned the move to promote Miller will only worsen relations between the White House and Capitol Hill.

“The president has two directions, one was to work with the Democratic Congress to try to get some things done. The other is to go to war with them. Stephen is more of a go-to-war guy,” the lobbyist said.

But Grogan argued that Trump’s move to tap Miller as his chief of staff could be seen as a negotiating tactic in itself.

“Trump is a negotiator and by picking Miller he is negotiating because he’s projecting strength, not weakness,” Grogan said.

articles.title: The Memo: GOP fumbles for way forward in a world beyond Trump
articles.summary: A historic election week is ending, but the debate about the future of the Republican Party is just beginning. On one side are those who see the midterms as a wholesale repudiation of President Trump — or at least a startling reminder that neither he nor his party is immune to the laws of political…
articles.body:
A historic election week is ending, but the debate about the future of the Republican Party is just beginning.

On one side are those who see the midterms as a wholesale repudiation of President Trump — or at least a startling reminder that neither he nor his party is immune to the laws of political gravity.

According to this theory, everything from Trump’s war on Iran to his solipsistic rhetoric about White House renovations weighed heavily on voters who were mostly concerned with the cost of living.

On the other side of the internal divide are those who urge their party colleagues not to overreact or overcorrect. This faction believes that, while some minor course corrections may be necessary, the right-wing populism that Trump espouses retains broad appeal.

These aren’t just abstract debates, of course.

Since Tuesday’s cataclysm — where GOP-held Senate seats were lost even in crimson strongholds like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina — potential 2028 standard-bearers have been offering their prognosis about what went wrong. The implicit message in the responses from Vice President Vance, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), among others, is that they are the people to put it right.

Vance, on social media , wrote, “The reason we lost is the war” — a very thinly veiled reminder that he is perceived as a skeptic about the conflict.

DeSantis lamented at a press conference that the results were “close to an extinction-level event” — but noted that his Florida was “the one state that was able to hold the line.”

Cruz, in a lengthy post on social platform X , highlighted how the GOP had alienated Hispanic voters and emphasized his record in winning their support.

The battle to define the GOP’s future direction, and to determine who leads it into the 2028 election, looks set to be fierce.

For the moment, Trump critics are feeling validated.

Former Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson (R) told this column that the election results were a manifestation of “defiance” from the electorate against Trump’s “style and chaos.”

Hutchinson, who ran a long-shot campaign against Trump for the GOP nomination in 2024, said that his party now had an opening to “not simply be a mirror image of President Trump, which it has been, really, for the past 10 years.”

Beyond questions about Trump himself, Hutchinson argued that a change in direction was imperative for the Republican Party’s electoral self-preservation — and that such a move was possible without any abandonment of conservative values.

“We have to be in a position to win the votes of those in the middle — and the new generation of voters,” he said. “That takes change and adjustment, but it’s not a violation of fundamental principles.”

At the other end of the GOP’s spectrum are the Trump loyalists who disdain such anxieties and say the best response to Tuesday’s results is to keep rolling down the MAGA road — regardless of how much liberal outrage or media criticism this generates.

This camp takes heart from Trump’s announcement Friday afternoon that Stephen Miller is to become White House chief of staff , replacing the departing Susie Wiles.

To say Miller is controversial is an understatement.

He is widely seen as the main architect of the administration’s immigration enforcement policies, an advocate of extremely expansive executive powers, a fierce critic of judges who have the temerity to rule against the president, and a pugnacious cable-news brawler — among other things.

“I’m going to miss Susie [Wiles] a lot, but we’re now at war and Stephen Miller is a wartime consigliere,” longtime Trump adviser Michael Caputo told this column, suggesting there is a need to gird for battle with a Democratic-controlled Congress.

Caputo, who demurred on discussing the battle for the 2028 GOP nomination, argued that the Trump administration needed to intensify its focus. He said this pattern had already been seen in the past from Democrats, when then-President Obama endured significant midterm defeats for his party.

“I would counsel that, like Obama, we double down,” Caputo said. “And there’s nobody better to double down with than Stephen Miller.”

Others draw different lessons from the midterms — even if they acknowledge such talk is taking place against the backdrop of a president who reacts volcanically to criticism and a GOP base that is still supportive of him.

“Everybody is delicately weighing in, everybody’s discussing this privately — consultants, candidates, everyone,” said Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based GOP strategist who is also the CEO of the Alliance for Secure AI.

“Clearly, Ted Cruz and Marco Rubio and JD [Vance] and Ron DeSantis are doing similar: ‘What are the takeaways from the election? What are we confident in saying about the election? If we feel the need to be more critical of the president, is it a bad idea if we step out?’ Everyone is having those conversations.”

The strategist said his view was that the cost of living hurt the GOP more than anything else, but that a host of other topics — from the war to the exponential growth of data centers to concerns about corruption — also played on voters’ minds.

But Steinhauser was frank in admitting it’s too early to say what it all means for 2028.

“I don’t want to overstate it,” he said. “There are all these articles saying ‘MAGA is dead’ but the base is going to be with Trump. It’s so hard to predict, but it would be the wrong analysis to think they want a George W. Bush-type figure.”

The mere fact that Trump suffered such an electoral rebuke in the midterms perhaps complicates Vance’s position more than anyone else’s.

His message blaming the war for the GOP’s defeat was widely seen as an effort to create distance from Trump without seeming disloyal. It’s not clear if it’s possible to thread this needle over a longer period.

Doug Heye, a GOP strategist and former communications director of the Republican National Committee, noted that Vance was hardly the first vice president to face this challenge.

In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris’s remark, during an interview with ABC’s “The View,” that there was “not a thing” she would have done differently from then-President Biden came to haunt her.

“These are very difficult waters,” Heye said. “It’s like watching the Olympics — sometimes it’s hard to say whether something is possible until someone does it, until someone sticks the landing.”

“That’s where Republicans are right now,” he added. “They’re in the air, spinning. And we don’t know how, or who, can stick the landing.”

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: We talked to dozens of voters about the midterm results. Here’s what they want to see now
articles.summary: Fear was the word Daisy Alcazar used most during an October visit CNN’s All Over the Map made to her ice cream shop near the US-Mexico border in South Texas.
articles.body:
Fear was the word Daisy Alcazar used most during an October visit CNN's All Over the Map made to her ice cream shop near the US-Mexico border in South Texas.

Hope is what she voices most now, when she can stop crying tears of joy.

"Texas has turned BLUE!" Alcazar wrote in a celebratory post-election message.

"The Latino community showed up," she said later. "We have the first Latina woman going into the governor's mansion. Do you understand what that means?"

Joseph Knowles was on the losing side of the midterm reckoning. He is a union autoworker in Michigan, voted Republican and watched as the map for governor, Senate and his House district filled in blue.

"I'm disappointed and Trump shares the blame," Knowles said of the results. "Hopefully Democrats will use their power to deliver real change, not political revenge."

Alcazar and Knowles are among more the 150 voters who participate in our All Over the Map project, an effort to track elections and major issues through the eyes and experiences of everyday Americans.

Our travels these past 20 months, since Trump returned to the White House, took us to 15 states from Maine to Alaska, some two or three times, and to many of the places that delivered the most stunning and consequential change.

"The voters have put checks and balances back in place," said Michele Pegg, the Democratic chairwoman in rural Louisa County, Iowa. Democrats flipped the governor's office, a Senate seat and three of Iowa's four House districts, including the 1st District, where we visited with Pegg twice in recent months.

"Serve the public – don't forget that," was her morning-after message.

Some of the responses to a survey sent to our voters on Election Day and a follow-up Wednesday were illuminating and reinforced a giant lesson since we began All Over The Map 38 months ago.

The Democrats in our project are obviously gleeful and the Republicans predictably disappointed. But voters across the spectrum are willing and eager to search for consensus on the big issues and blame the politicians for exacerbating polarization instead of making tough choices.

"The majority of the voters are not as extreme as the officials who get elected," said Joan London, an attorney in Berks County, Pennsylvania, who switched her registration from Republican to independent in 2024 after Trump clinched the Republican nomination for the third time.

An example: Chris Mudd is a Trump supporter since 2015 and voted a straight Republican ballot Tuesday in Iowa. Alcazar is the Texas Democrat who loathes Trump.

During a Zoom conversation Friday, Mudd nodded in agreement as Alcazar voiced hope the midterm upheaval might somehow create momentum for a new guest worker program and creating a path to legal status for undocumented workers who have no criminal history since illegally crossing the border.

"We need the work to get done," said Mudd, who since the beginning of our project in the summer of 2023 has listed border security as his top priority. "There are workers that want to come do it. We should have a plan to bring them in to do the work."

Across party lines, there are voters who expect more gridlock and inaction regardless of which party controls Congress.

"Time for Washington to go back to going around in circles chasing each other's tails," said Deven McIver, a heavy equipment operator and New Hampshire Republican.

"Term limits, maximum age for Congress and Senate," is part of the wish list sent by Craig Thomas, a coastal South Carolina Republican.

"Speak out specifically for anti-corruption legislation by passing anti-stock and prediction market investment by members (of Congress) and federal employees," was a priority Maine Democrat Brenda Garrand listed for the next Congress. Garrand said her "most important action" would be to "gut Citizens United," the landmark Supreme Court decision that helped usher in a new era of big money in American elections.

Latinos feel empowered in Texas and beyond

"Enjoying the Bright Blue moment in Nevada," said Las Vegas real estate agent Zoila Sanchez, a onetime Reagan Republican who switched parties because of Trump.

"Latino voices must be heard," said Rogelio Regalado, a Spanish-language radio host in Nevada.

"We showed up at the ballot box, now we expect them to show up for us," said Victor Martinez, a Spanish-language radio personality in Allentown, Pennsylvania.

"JoAnna Mendoza unseating Juan Ciscomani is everything," said Melissa Cordero, an Air Force veteran who lives in Tucson, Arizona. Mendoza is a Democrat who defeated Republican Ciscomani in the 6th Congressional District.

"Now we have two badass Latinas, Adelita Grijalva and JoAnna Mendoza, on the Hill to make better decisions for Arizona and Tucson and especially for veterans," Cordero said.

"Impeachment proceedings will be a hot-button issue," said Ed Winebarger, a farmer and chef in western North Carolina. "I hope we can make it happen."

Emily Bruce Plumb, a Maine Democrat and brand management expert, has a very different take.

"My biggest fear is that Democrats will waste their shot by getting caught up in impeachment dramas," said Plumb. "I want them to take the high road and do the most good for the people and stay out of personal vendettas or acts of retribution."

Some Republicans expect Democrats to push for impeachment.

"I see two years of anti-Trump rhetoric, impeachment-palooza and none of the important things we American citizens want," said Debbie Katsanos, a New Hampshire Republican.

Leadership doubts are also an issue for the winning team.

"Please don't let this end up being two years that end with another Republican president," said Mary Ann Horvath, a Pennsylvania retiree. "Choose stronger and better leaders than Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries."

Anushka Jalisatgi, a law student in Michigan, said El-Sayed's win in Michigan adds to the momentum progressives received from the election of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. "The status quo establishment Democratic position is not permanent," she said.

South Carolina Republican Billy Pierce said high gas prices powered the revolt against the GOP and that they were the result of a war "that Trump promised the United States would not keep getting drawn into." Plus, he said Trump's choice of Darline Graham to replace her late brother as the Senate candidate in his state "was a fiasco from the start."

In Texas, Marine veteran Richard Contreras said he voted "red and (is) somewhat ashamed by it" because he sees the party drifting from conservative and moral principles.

"I went to a Trump rally in Corpus Christi, and I didn't or I wasn't able to identify with anyone in the crowd," Contreras said. "It was almost cult like."

Mudd, the Iowa Republican, was one of a number of longtime Trump loyalists who late in this campaign began to share more concerns about his conduct.

"I think we need to have laws that we all live by, including the president," Mudd said. "I think the president needs to follow all the laws. I'm not so far on Trump that he can do anything that he wants to do, and I'll be okay with it. I want our country to run the way it did when I was a kid."

Michael Pesce was a Reagan Republican until Trump emerged. He has voted for the Democrat every time Trump was on the presidential ballot, but in every one of those elections he also voted for moderate GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick in Pennsylvania's 1st Congressional District. This week, stopping Trump mattered most.

"I was sitting in the booth with my hand hovering over Fitzpatrick's name, like this is where it's supposed to go, but I just couldn't bring myself to do it," Pesce said. He had plenty of company in a district Fitzpatrick easily won two years ago. "I think in this area …. people were like, "Nope, we're gonna change this."

Of course, the next campaign begins as soon as the current one ends. Can Democrats hold these big gains? How will the 2026 reckoning impact the 2028 presidential nomination contests? How will the volatile electorate that delivered Trump a stunning comeback in 2024 only to repudiate him and crumble his coalition two years later feel the next time?

"I want my party back," is the early marker placed by Pesce. "The race for president starts now and I hope whoever is considering running learned a lesson from the past two years."

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

articles.title: Peltola campaign sues Alaska over rejected absentee ballot records
articles.summary: Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign is suing the state of Alaska to obtain access to records for absentee ballots that were rejected by the Alaska Division of Elections, a new court filing shows. Peltola’s campaign said they previously requested records of the rejected ballots on multiple occasions but were denied access. “Plaintiff cannot ensure that its…
articles.body:
Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign is suing the state of Alaska to obtain access to records for absentee ballots that were rejected by the Alaska Division of Elections, a new court filing shows.

Peltola’s campaign said they previously requested records of the rejected ballots on multiple occasions but were denied access.

“Plaintiff cannot ensure that its voters’ lawful votes were properly counted without knowing whose absentee ballots were rejected or questioned, and why,” the lawsuit reads. “Each hour and each day that Defendants deny Plaintiff the requested records to which it is entitled costs Plaintiff the opportunity to help ensure that qualified voters have their ballots counted.”

Peltola currently leads Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) in the Alaska U.S. Senate race by just over 600 votes, but with approximately 30 percent of the vote still outstanding, according to The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). No winner has been projected in the race as of Saturday morning.

The Division responded in a release on Friday, saying voters who have had their ballots rejected have not yet had access to the information, therefore, the campaign should not be able to have access yet either.

“Alaska’s constitution and laws do not require the Division to provide this information in the manner requested by the campaign. Releasing preliminary information in the manner sought by the lawsuit would create additional burdens during ballot processing and could delay the timely counting of votes,” the release said.

The Alaska Senate race has already been the subject of litigation after the Trump administration sued to block certification of the election if Sullivan loses, arguing that the presence of a candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. could confuse voters. A judge dismissed that lawsuit ahead of Election Day, but the administration vowed to appeal.

The vote count in Alaska will continue for several more days , as ballots in Alaska can arrive up to 15 days after the election if they came from outside the country, so long as they are postmarked by Election Day.

More votes in Alaska do not have to be reported until Nov. 10, but may be reported incrementally before then. Final votes must be reported by Nov. 18.

If no candidate has greater than 50 percent of the vote by that point — no candidate currently does — the state will run an instant runoff using ranked choice voting. The tabulation eliminates the last-place candidate and redistributes their voters’ second, third and fourth-choice preferences. The process repeats until a candidate has a majority.

If Peltola wins the Senate race, it would be the eighth flip for Democrats in the Senate after a strong performance on Tuesday night.

Votes are also still being counted in the Mississippi Senate contest where Democrat Scott Colom leads the incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

articles.title: Who is Hakeem Jeffries, the Democrat poised to become House speaker?
articles.summary: Likely to become the first Black House speaker, Jeffries faces pressure from progressives over Trump and Israel.
articles.body:
With Democrats’ decisive victory in the United States’ midterm elections on Tuesday, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York is on the verge of making history as the first Black speaker of the US House of Representatives.

For the 56-year-old congressman, it would be the culmination of almost two decades in office, giving him a central role in Democrats’ efforts to rein in Republican US President Donald Trump in the final two years of his presidency.

But as Jeffries celebrated the “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats back into power the day after the election, some within the party were not convinced that the congressman, known for his cautious approach to politics and longstanding support for Israel, was the right man for the moment.

An online petition on Change.org calling on lawmakers to choose another speaker had collected more than 980,000 signatures by Saturday morning, while several newly elected progressive lawmakers have not said whether they will support him.

“We believe the Speaker should represent the Democratic voters, not just the Democratic establishment,” the petition reads.

“This is not a foregone conclusion,” it continues, urging others to run for the job.

Jeffries, who has spent years cultivating relationships within the Democratic caucus, now finds himself at the centre of a bigger fight within the party, as its growing progressive wing pushes for a more confrontational approach to Trump and a break with some of the ideas that have defined the Democrats for decades.

Jeffries grew up in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, in the 1970s and 1980s, as the neighbourhood was grappling with the crack cocaine epidemic.

“There was a lot of dysfunction and pain that surrounded the communities that I was raised in, but also a lot of love and compassion from family and friends, and community folks,” he told NYU Law in 2019.

The son of two social workers, Jeffries eventually became a lawyer, tracing his decision to pursue a career in law back to the 1992 riots that erupted in Los Angeles after four white police officers were acquitted in the beating of Rodney King, a Black man.

“It crystallized the fact that we still had a long way to go to eradicate social and racial injustice,” he said.

Jeffries went on to work as a corporate lawyer before entering politics, losing two runs for the New York State Assembly before winning a seat in 2006 and eventually being elected to Congress six years later.

In Washington, he helped broker a bipartisan criminal justice reform law signed by Trump in 2018. Two years later, during Trump’s first impeachment trial, he argued that Trump should be removed from office as one of seven House impeachment managers who presented the case to the US Senate.

Rising quickly through the Democratic ranks, Jeffries became caucus chair in 2019 before making history three years later, when he was unanimously chosen to succeed former Speaker Nancy Pelosi as the party’s House leader, becoming the first Black politician to lead a party in either chamber of Congress.

Jeffries and Pelosi have been compared for their distinct leadership styles. While Pelosi was known for her commanding, top-down approach, Jeffries has built a reputation for quietly and deliberately building consensus among his colleagues.

That approach has frustrated some Democrats, who say Jeffries has been too reluctant to take firm positions and who question whether he is prepared to confront Trump and Republicans in Congress aggressively enough.

Those concerns were on display after Jeffries declared after the election that “the American people don’t want us to get even; they want us to get things done on their behalf.”

Among those who pushed back was left-wing political commentator Hasan Piker, who reposted a video of Jeffries’s comments, saying: “No, we definitely ARE looking for justice and accountability.”

Jeffries also faced criticism after reports emerged in August that he had privately met Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, who does not have a formal role in the administration but has been involved in diplomatic efforts in the Middle East and in Russia.

Jeffries defended the meeting, saying Kushner had requested it and that he had used it to discuss the affordability crisis. But critics argued that rather than meeting privately with Kushner, Jeffries should have been preparing to investigate his business dealings.

Ahead of the election, Axios reported on a plan by some incoming progressive lawmakers – informally known as “The Bloc” and including Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York and Melat Kiros of Colorado – to use the upcoming speaker vote to win concessions from Jeffries on issues such as Medicare for All, cutting funding for ICE, and weapons shipments to Israel.

That may be harder now that the Democrats have a comfortable majority, with Jeffries less dependent on progressive newcomers to secure the speakership. But the result also makes it harder for Jeffries to argue, as he has in the past, that Republican control of Congress is hindering the Democrats’ ability to advance their agenda and hold Trump accountable.

Jeffries’s Israel stance divides Democrats

Of all the sources of tension between Jeffries and his party’s progressive wing, the hardest divide to bridge may be over his longstanding support for Israel and ties to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).

At a conference hosted by the group in 2020, Jeffries opposed putting conditions on US aid to Israel and described Jerusalem as New York City’s “sixth borough”.

He has also been one of the top recipients of financial support from AIPAC and its network of donors, earning the nickname “AIPAC Shakur” from New York radio host Charlamagne tha God.

In a celebratory post after the elections congratulating the candidates it had supported, AIPAC singled out Jeffries and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer by name.

But Jeffries’s steadfast support for Israel throughout its genocidal war on Gaza has put him increasingly at odds with his own party, and he recently signalled that his position may be changing.

In July, even as he voted against an amendment that would have cut $3.3bn in annual military aid to Israel, he acknowledged the need for a reset in US-Israel relations.

“A meaningful change in direction is needed,” he wrote in a letter to colleagues.

Jeffries appears to have the speakership all but secured, with no serious challenger emerging so far.

However, with Trump still in the White House, a party grappling with its own divisions, and voters expecting change on everything from the cost of living to the war on Iran, the bigger test for Jeffries will come once he is on the job.

First Lady Melania Trump is set to attend to the college football face-off between Louisiana State University and the University of Alabama Saturday afternoon, a visit tied to her Fostering the Future education initiative.

The White House announced earlier this week the first lady had awarded LSU $5 million to establish a permanent endowment fund providing scholarships to students in the foster care system. LSU will play Alabama at 3 p.m. EST in Baton Rouge, La.

Meanwhile, President Trump is in Mar-a-Lago — where the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) is hosting the final day of its Circle Retreat and Gala on the heels of several stunning GOP losses during Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Among guests at the multi-day retreat, which began on Nov. 4, many have recently faced public controversies — such as newly-appointed White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, ousted former U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and right-wing Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, who fled the country following his election loss.

In battleground Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign is suing the state to obtain access to records for absentee ballots that were rejected by the Alaska Division of Elections.

A new court filing shows Peltola’s campaign previously requested records of the rejected ballots on multiple occasions but were denied access.

Peltola currently leads Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) in the Alaska U.S. Senate race by just over 600 votes, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The president has a policy meeting scheduled for 6:30 p.m. EST and does not have any public appearances listed on his schedule.
