articles.title: The Amish versus New York: When vaccine mandates clash with faith
articles.summary: The U.S. Supreme Court is now the only remedy for the Amish. But history, basic decency and precedent are on their side.
articles.body:
Amish families began settling in New York as early as the 1830s , drawn, like so many before them, by the promise of religious liberty. For nearly two centuries they have farmed the land, built their own schools and asked little of their neighbors. The Supreme Court once called them “good farmers and citizens.”

Today, New York is penalizing them for simply practicing their faith.

The facts are simple. Three small Old Order Amish schools, funded solely by the Amish, located on Amish farms and attended only by Amish children, are attended by families who hold a sincere religious objection to vaccination. For more than 50 years , from 1966 to 2019, New York respected that objection through a religious accommodation in state law. Shortly after the state repealed the accommodation, for the first time in the Amish community’s long history in New York, the state charged the schools with violations and imposed $118,000 in penalties.

During debate over the repeal, the bill’s sponsors dismissed religious beliefs as “fake” and “garbage.” That is not the language of neutrality.

The U.S. Supreme Court is now the only remedy for the Amish . But history, basic decency and precedent are on their side.

In Wisconsin v. Yoder , the Supreme Court held that Amish parents have a protected right to direct the religious upbringing of their children, even against a generally applicable state law. Recent decisions by the court in Mahmoud v. Taylor and Mirabelli v. Bonta reaffirmed that lower courts may not shrink Yoder to its specific facts. Vaccination is a permanent, irreversible act, exactly the kind of compelled step against conscience that no later ruling can undo. Even the Second Circuit conceded the burden is “serious.”

In addition, the relevant New York law is neither neutral nor generally applicable. New York allows a medical exemption that turns on the judgment of doctors and school officials. The vaccine requirement does not reach teachers, aides or administrators in public schools, yet the state has targeted Amish school children.

And, by the state’s own estimate, as many as 97,900 students in New York remain unvaccinated without any exemption — almost four times the entire Amish population of New York . When a state tolerates that much secular noncompliance but will not tolerate a religious objection, it must justify itself under strict scrutiny. Under Tandon v. Newsom , comparable secular activity cannot be treated better than religious exercise.

A denial of religious accommodation for the Amish leaves them with only two choices — pay ruinous fines or leave New York. Forty-five other states and the District of Columbia allow religious exemptions . New York is an outlier.

The Amish did not seek this conflict. Their representative wrote that they are “sincerely sorry” to be causing the state a problem, that they desire a quiet, peaceful life and hold respect for authority, but that when law conflicts with scripture, they must obey God rather than man. Litigation is their last resort, and they feel shame at being cast as aggressors.

Yoder called forced migration of religious minorities “an evil that lay at the heart of the Religion Clauses.” A state that drives out the Amish would repeat exactly that evil. Free exercise means little if it protects only popular faiths. Accommodation cost New York nothing for half a century.

The Amish have long been a litmus test of our commitment to religious liberty. The court should ensure New York passes that test.

Kelly Shackelford is president, CEO and chief counsel for First Liberty Institute , a nonprofit law firm dedicated to defending religious freedom for all.

articles.title: Newsom’s death-row commutations spark DA revolt as prosecutors warn of legal fight
articles.summary: California district attorneys accuse Gavin Newsom of overriding juries and ignoring victims' families with his plan to commute all 548 death sentences in the state.
articles.body: At least a dozen California district attorneys are publicly condemning Gov. Gavin Newsom’s plan to commute all 548 death sentences in the state, arguing the sweeping move overrides juries, disregards victims’ families and defies the will of state voters. Newsom announced the plan Thursday, saying state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values. The move would convert the sentences to life without parole, though 382 cases still require approval from at least four California Supreme Court justices, according to the Associated Press. In response, prosecuting attorneys across California have raised concerns about victims’ rights, the governor’s constitutional authority and the role of the California Supreme Court in reviewing hundreds of the commutations. "Justice requires case-by-case consideration, not one-size-fits-all decisions," Sacramento County District Attorney Thien Ho said in response to Newsom's action. THREE STATES CARRY OUT EXECUTIONS ON SAME DAY AMID RENEWED DEATH PENALTY DEBATE Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer described the move as "mercy for the wolves" that inflicts "the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep." Spitzer noted that regulations implemented by California’s Board of Parole Hearings on Oct. 1 allow thousands of prisoners serving life without parole to become eligible for parole, arguing that Newsom's latest death row commutations could put these inmates "one step closer" to release. Newsom’s office says, however, that the affected prisoners will remain in prison and are not eligible for release. "The Governor is attempting to appear courageous with this decision. He is not courageous. His commutations are solely based upon power and political aspirations," added San Bernardino County District Attorney Jason Anderson, who accused Newsom of caring more about politics than people. "Courage would require speaking with crime victims and the surviving family members of the people murdered by these death row inmates." CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM Anderson cited the case of Kevin Cooper, a California death-row inmate convicted of killing Josh Ryen’s parents and sister, along with Ryen’s friend, Chris Hughes, and leaving Ryen for dead. Anderson said Newsom had not contacted Ryen or Hughes’ mother, Mary Ann Hughes, to ask their views on a possible commutation — and that Ryen has never received a call from the governor. "Courage would require the Governor to follow Marsy’s Law, California’s constitutional rights belonging to victims of crime," Anderson continued. "He has not. I am not aware of any victims’ family members receiving notice of these commutations from the Governor." Meanwhile, Anderson and several other California prosecutors who spoke out against Newsom's death row commutations also framed the dispute as a challenge to the jury system and an override of the will of California voters. They said jurors in each case heard the evidence, weighed all the necessary factors and decided whether death was warranted, with judges and appellate courts later reviewing those verdicts. Newsom’s blanket action, they argue, substitutes one statewide decision for hundreds of individualized judgments. NEW YORK BILLS COULD ABOLISH LIFE WITHOUT PAROLE FOR SERIAL KILLERS AND COP KILLERS, CRITICS WARN "A single order commuting all of them would set aside hundreds of individualized judgments without examining the facts of even one," San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow said. "It invalidates the exhausting, emotionally wrenching work of our citizens who sat on juries, weighed horrific evidence, and delivered lawful verdicts. Most unforgivably, it is a slap in the face to victims and their families," said San Joaquin District Attorney Ron Freitas. "This decision does not bind wounds; it tears them wide open, all over again." The prosecutors pointed out that California voters rejected death-penalty repeal initiatives in 2012 and 2016 while approving Proposition 66 in 2016, which changed procedures for challenging death sentences and was promoted by supporters as a way to speed up the process. The district attorneys argued Newsom’s blanket action overrides those ballot-box decisions without repealing the law. "A blanket commutation is a mass erasure of justice. It overrides the will of California voters who have repeatedly defended capital punishment at the ballot box," Freitas added in his response to Newsom's action. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Some California prosecutors who spoke out against Newsom's controversial move signaled that the dispute may not end with public statements. San Diego County District Attorney Summer Stephan said her office was "researching any lawful remedies" that would allow victims’ voices to be heard and considered, while Kern County District Attorney Cynthia Zimmer was more direct, saying, "This assault on justice will be challenged." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman acknowledged that commuting existing sentences falls within the governor’s constitutional authority, but said, "That power does not extend to eliminating the death penalty. Only the Legislature or the voters can do that." Newsom’s clemency announcement clarifies that it "does not repeal the death penalty" and is limited to commuting California’s current death sentences. Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment but did not hear back in time for publication.

articles.title: A ‘reverse-Ginsberg’ scenario could flip the Supreme Court without packing
articles.summary: In Henry VI, Shakespeare wrote, “Defer no time, delays have dangerous ends.” Many today would like to chisel those words above the doors to the Supreme Court. Time and time again, justices waited too long for their own legacies. For many conservatives, the decisive loss of both houses of Congress has created a true nightmare…
articles.body:
In Henry VI, Shakespeare wrote, “Defer no time, delays have dangerous ends.” Many today would like to chisel those words above the doors to the Supreme Court. Time and time again, justices waited too long for their own legacies.

For many conservatives, the decisive loss of both houses of Congress has created a true nightmare scenario in which two conservatives (Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito) could hand Democrats the opportunity to take control of the Supreme Court without having to carry out their court-packing schemes. Control of the court could now be lost by sheer attrition.

Timing has always been a looming question for justices who want to see their seats filled by like-minded jurists. However, it is difficult to walk away from being one of nine.

Some served beyond their own capabilities in clinging to the court, becoming befuddled and isolated with age. That was the case with iconic justices such as William Douglas and Thurgood Marshall.

Others stayed too long to guarantee the preservation of their own legacies. The most recent example is Ruth Bader Ginsburg. Some of us wrote for years that Ginsburg was risking her legacy by not retiring while Barack Obama was president. After President Trump replaced her with Justice Amy Coney Barrett, many liberals (who were consciously silent before her death) lamented her decision.

Now, conservatives worry they may face a double tap. For two years, there has been speculation that Thomas (78) and Alito (76) might retire to allow a Republican president and Republican Senate to select their successors. Both declined to do so.

If they were hoping for a two-year cushion, that window just closed with a resounding bang. Even if they were to resign in the next two years, it is unlikely that Trump could replace either with a conservative nominee.

With at least 54 Senate seats (and perhaps as many as 56), the Democrats do not fear defections from independent-minded senators like Sen. John Fetterman (D., N.J.). They will also cite the denial of a vote for Merrick Garland during the Obama administration as a justification for denying a vote to Trump nominees.

Even before the election, liberals had raised money to campaign against even prospective nominees for Trump.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris called for Democratic donors to oppose “additional justices” that might be nominated by Trump “before they happen.” She praised the fundraising by Josh Orton, president of the dark-money group “Demand Justice.” It was a notable endorsement, since Demand Justice was infamous for its campaign to get Justice Stephen Breyer to resign, including mobile billboards reading “Breyer, retire. Don’t risk your legacy.” Demand Justice has also pushed a radical agenda, including court-packing .

Of course, Breyer did resign, allowing Biden to replace him with Ketanji Brown Jackson, arguably the farthest-left justice to ever sit on the court.

As soon as the Democrats took control, the Senate Minority Leader (and possible incoming Majority Leader) Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) declared that they would bar “any crappy nominees,” which was taken to mean any Trump nominee.

In fairness to Thomas and Alito, neither is diminished by age. Both have appeared in public and shown they are fully capable and effective. In the cases of Douglass and Marshall, they were eventually pressured to resign after they appeared on television and were clearly enfeebled.

The last two years have seen some of the most important opinions from Thomas and Alito in their careers on the court. Now, however, they could be looking at not two more years but six more years to wait for a Republican president if the midterms foreshadow the 2028 election.

If so, by the time a Republican could succeed such a Democrat, Thomas would be roughly 84 and Alito 82. And the Senate may not even then be ready to confirm like-minded successors.

The risk is tremendous. If their vacancies cause a reverse Ginsburg, the court would shift from a 6-3 majority favoring conservatives to a 5-4 majority favoring liberals.

Worse yet, in the calls to pack the court with a liberal majority, politicians and pundits often point to Biden-appointee Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson as the model. Jackson has been widely criticized for a radical jurisprudence that discards longstanding norms and doctrines, including by her two liberal colleagues.

Such a court would make court packing entirely unnecessary. The signature opinions of Thomas and Alito would likely fall in quick succession, from Thomas’s gun rights decision in Bruen to Alito’s abortion ruling in Dobbs.

Nevertheless, it is much to ask for two jurists to resign when they are both mentally and physically capable, particularly after rendering some of their most influential opinions in the last two years.

Some believe that justices should not engage in strategic resignations to shape the ideology of the Court. These justices, they reason, have a right to serve out their lifetime appointments as long as they can do the job. They can have a clear conscience serving as long as they are able, and leave their replacements to the will of the American people.

In any case, with less than six weeks left with a Republican Senate, the time has effectively run out for the retirement option in holding these seats for conservatives.

The irony is that these two justices can take considerable credit in the building of the conservative jurisprudence that has emerged in recent years on the court. They have shown great patience in building the authority to overturn longstanding cases, from Roe v. Wade to Humphrey’s Executor . That legacy may now rest with their own longevity in the years to come.

articles.title: Miller calls chief of staff promotion ‘honor of my life’ at Mar-a-Lago event
articles.summary: Longtime White House aide Stephen Miller pledged his “absolute loyalty” to President Trump in short remarks Friday evening shortly after being promoted to chief of staff — replacing Susie Wiles “We need to stand with the man who has stood with us with every fiber of his being,” Miller said in a video Trump posted…
articles.body:
Longtime White House aide Stephen Miller pledged his “absolute loyalty” to President Trump in short remarks Friday evening shortly after being promoted to chief of staff — replacing Susie Wiles

“We need to stand with the man who has stood with us with every fiber of his being,” Miller said in a video Trump posted to Truth Social . “I pledge you, Mr. President, my absolute loyalty, my unwavering commitment and my total devotion to your success and the success of this country.”

Giving quick remarks at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Palm Beach, Fla., Miller called the promotion “the honor of my life.”

Trump announced Friday morning that Wiles, who had served as chief of staff since he returned to office, had stepped down and Miller would replace her.

The choice quickly sparked backlash from Democrats and some Republicans, who said the president learned the wrong lesson from sweeping midterm losses.

“Donald Trump learned nothing from his historic defeat,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) wrote in a post on the social platform X. “Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn’t have made a worse choice.”

Miller was the architect behind much of the president’s hardline immigration policies, including mass deportation efforts in his second term. Democrats have slammed Miller for his rhetoric in the past, namely after he called the two American citizens killed during federal immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis “domestic terrorists.”

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) said Friday the president should “rethink” his decision to elevate Miller, calling it a “colossal mistake” after the party’s midterm losses.

“This past Tuesday, Republicans lost because we lost the narrative on the border, a success that the president should have been heralding,” Tillis said. “Now we’re talking about putting one of the most partisan, polarizing figures, and not only polarizing in terms of Republicans and Democrats, but even among Republicans.”

Trump’s cabinet secretaries broadly praised the switch, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who shared a photo of himself and Miller with the caption , “Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic.”

Millers’s chief of staff appointment brings Hegseth even closer to the White House as the Pentagon chief faces growing backlash for his leadership and handling of the Iran war. House Oversight Committee chair James Comer (R-Ky.) admitted , “There’s a lot of questions about Hegseth” as Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) renews his push to impeach the defense secretary.

But Miller seemed to sing the praises of the second Trump administration’s defense agenda Friday night, saying, “If it wasn’t for President Trump, the United States of America would not exist right now. This man saved America. He saved our military from collapse. He saved our economy from destruction. He saved our boarder from annihilation. And he saved our country from threats from home and abroad.”
